name: Security and Risk Management
plainMeaning: This domain is about how an organization decides what to protect, how much to spend, and who is responsible. It covers ethics, laws, policies, people and risk, which are the management foundations for all other security work.

topics.name: Professional ethics and the ISC2 Code
topics.simpleExplanation: Security people are trusted with secrets, money and the keys to important systems. So they must behave well. ISC2, the organization that runs the CISSP exam, has a code of ethics that every certified member must follow. It has four rules, called canons, and they come in a fixed order. Society comes first, then honest and legal behaviour, then your employer or client, then the profession. Your workplace will also have its own code of ethics. You must follow both, and you must help others follow them too.

studyNotes.heading: Why ethics matters in security
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at why ethics matters so much in security work. Let us begin with something familiar.

Think of a locksmith. A locksmith can open almost any door in town. People only call one they trust. If a locksmith copied keys, or told burglars which houses were empty, the whole trade would suffer.

Now think about your own work. A security professional can often see private files, staff records and bank data. An administrator at a hospital may be able to open any patient record. An analyst at a bank may watch the traffic that carries customer payments. Nobody checks every action these people take. The organization simply has to trust them.

Ethics means knowing what is right and doing it, even when nobody is watching. Ethics is not quite the same thing as law. Something can be legal and still be wrong. Your monitoring tools may lawfully capture a colleague's private message. That does not make it right to read it out of curiosity.

ISC2 is the organization that runs this certification. The letters stand for the International Information System Security Certification Consortium. The certification is the CISSP, which means Certified Information Systems Security Professional. Everyone who holds it agrees to follow the ISC2 Code of Professional Ethics. Following the Code is a condition of keeping the certification.

The Code begins with a short opening statement called the preamble. A preamble is an introduction that explains the purpose of what follows. In plain words, it says that the safety and welfare of society and the common good, our duty to the people we serve, and our duty to each other, require us to hold the highest standards of behaviour. It also says we must be seen to hold them. That last part matters. Looking honest counts as well as being honest, because trust depends on what other people can see.

So here is what to take away. Security people hold unusual power over other people's information. Ethics is what makes that power safe, and the Code asks you both to behave well and to be seen to behave well.

studyNotes.heading: The four canons, in exact order
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the heart of the Code, which is its four canons. A canon is a main rule. You must know these in order, because the order is what settles a conflict.

- Canon 1: Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure.
- Canon 2: Act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally.
- Canon 3: Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
- Canon 4: Advance and protect the profession.

Let us walk through them slowly.

Canon 1 is about everybody. Society means the public at large. Infrastructure means the big systems that people depend on, like power, water, transport and hospitals. Public trust means people's confidence that these systems and the people who run them are sound.

Canon 2 is about your own conduct. Honourably means with integrity. Justly means fairly. Legally means obeying the law. Telling the truth in a report, even when the truth is unwelcome, is Canon 2.

Canon 3 is about the people who pay you. A principal is the person or organization you work for, such as your employer or a client. Diligent means careful and hard-working. Competent means having the skill to do the job.

Canon 4 is about your fellow professionals. You help the profession by sharing knowledge, mentoring newcomers and refusing to bring it into disrepute.

Here is an everyday picture. Imagine circles getting smaller. The biggest circle is the whole world. Inside it is your own honesty and the law. Inside that is your boss. The smallest circle is your own profession.

And here is a workplace picture. A consultant writes a report for a client. The report must not put the public in danger, which is Canon 1. It must be truthful, which is Canon 2. It must be careful and skilled work, which is Canon 3. And it must not embarrass the profession, which is Canon 4.

The point to take away is simple. Learn the four canons word for word and in order: society, honesty and law, principals, profession.

studyNotes.heading: When the canons clash
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at what you do when two canons pull in different directions. The rule is short. The higher canon wins. The harder skill is acting on it sensibly.

Start with an everyday case. Your friend asks you to keep a secret, and you are glad to. Then you learn the secret is that the brakes on the school bus do not work. Loyalty to your friend is real, but children's safety is more important. You would speak up, and you would speak to the right person.

Now a workplace case, worked through step by step. You are a consultant for a company that makes heart monitors. You discover that the monitors can be switched off remotely. The sales director asks you to leave this out of your report until after a big contract is signed.

First, name the duties. Your duty to the client is Canon 3. Your duty to tell the truth is Canon 2. Your duty to patients is Canon 1.

Second, rank them. Canon 1 is at the top, so patient safety decides the matter.

Third, choose the responsible route. You keep the finding in your report. You raise it in writing with senior management. You press for a fix and a safety notice. If the company refuses, you take legal advice and use the proper route to inform the regulator, which is the government body that oversees that industry.

Notice what you do not do. You do not rush to social media. Publishing the details could arm attackers and hurt the very patients you want to protect. You also do not quietly change the client's systems yourself, because you have no authority to do that.

This is how the exam wants you to think. You are an adviser and a manager, not a lone hero. You stay calm, you use the process, and you put people's safety first.

So remember this. When duties collide, the higher canon decides what matters most, and proper written escalation decides how you act on it.

studyNotes.heading: Living the canons at work
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at what the canons mean on an ordinary working day, when nothing dramatic is happening. Most ethics questions are small ones.

Begin with competence, which belongs to Canon 3. Think of a family doctor. If you need brain surgery, a good family doctor sends you to a surgeon. A bad one has a go. Security is the same. Suppose a client asks you to review the control systems in a factory, and you have never worked with them. The ethical move is to say so, and either bring in a specialist or decline the work. Never accept a job you are not qualified to do.

Now think about honesty, which belongs to Canon 2. Honest work means never overstating your skills or your results. If a test covered only half of the network, your report must say that. If you made a mistake that caused an outage, you say so.

Confidentiality toward clients also sits here. What you learn on one job does not travel to the next one. You do not take a former client's design documents to your new employer.

A conflict of interest is a situation where your private gain could affect your work decision. Imagine a referee whose brother plays for one of the teams. Even if the referee is perfectly fair, nobody will believe it. At work, this might be choosing a supplier whose director is your spouse, or accepting an expensive gift during a tender. A tender is a formal competition for a contract. The correct response is to declare the interest and step away from the decision.

Finally, there is Canon 4. You support the profession when you mentor a junior colleague, share lessons learned and treat others with respect. You harm it when you cheat. Certification fraud, and sharing the contents of the real exam, both damage the value of the credential for everyone.

Take this away. Ethics is mostly daily habits: admit what you cannot do, report truthfully, declare conflicts, and protect the good name of the profession.

studyNotes.heading: The organization's own code of ethics
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the second item in this objective, the organization's own code of ethics. The exam expects you to know that you follow both codes, and that you help to promote them.

A code of ethics is a written set of rules about right and wrong behaviour. Think of a football club. The league has its rules for every club. The club also has its own rules about how its players behave. A player must follow both.

In the same way, your employer will usually have its own code. It often covers honest dealing, gifts and hospitality, conflicts of interest, the treatment of colleagues, and the proper use of company property. It may be stricter than the ISC2 Code on some matters. A bank may ban all gifts from suppliers, for example, while the ISC2 Code says nothing about the size of a gift.

A code only works when certain things are in place. Think about them as a chain. Senior management approves it and follows it visibly, because staff copy what leaders do. Every member of staff receives it and agrees to it. People are trained on what it means in real situations. There is a safe way to report a concern, so that nobody fears punishment for speaking up. And the rules are enforced fairly, for junior staff and senior staff alike.

Here is a workplace example. A company publishes a fine code of ethics. Then a senior director is caught taking supplier gifts, and nothing happens. From that day, staff stop taking the code seriously. The fault is not in the wording. The fault is in the lack of leadership and enforcement.

Your part as a security professional is to promote the code by your own example. You also help to build it into the security program, through policy, awareness training and reporting channels.

So the thing to remember is this. A written code means little by itself. Leadership support, training, safe reporting and fair enforcement are what bring it to life.

studyNotes.heading: Complaints and consequences
studyNotes.body:
In this last part, we will look at what happens when someone breaks the ISC2 Code, and how to choose the best answer in an ethics question.

A member who knowingly breaks the Code can face a formal complaint and a review by ISC2. The result can be loss of the certification. Think of a doctor who can be struck off the medical register. The certificate is a public promise, so it can be taken back.

Complaints are made in writing, to ISC2, with supporting evidence. Members are expected to use this procedure when they see a breach of the Code. Spreading rumours is not the procedure. Neither is posting accusations online. The person complaining must have been affected by the conduct.

Who may complain depends on the canon. This is a detail worth learning.

- Canons 1 and 2: any member of the public.
- Canon 3: only principals, which means employers or clients.
- Canon 4: only other professionals.

Here is the reasoning behind it. Society's interests belong to everybody, so anybody can raise them. Service to a client concerns that client, so the client raises it. The good of the profession concerns professionals, so they raise it.

Consider a workplace case. You learn that a colleague who holds the certification has been altering audit results. You have evidence. You follow your employer's reporting route, because this is a business matter. You also make a formal complaint to ISC2 if the facts support it. You do not confront the colleague in public, and you do not threaten them.

When you meet an ethics question on the exam, use a short routine. Ask who could be harmed. Find the highest canon involved. Then pick the answer that is lawful, truthful and goes through a proper process. Be wary of answers that are dramatic, secret or based on revenge.

Here is your takeaway. Breaches go through the formal complaint process, who may complain depends on the canon, and the best answer is nearly always calm, honest and procedural.

topics.memoryHook: Society, Honesty, Boss, Peers. Think of circles shrinking from the whole world down to your own profession.

question.prompt: A security consultant working for a water company finds a flaw that could let attackers change the chemical levels in drinking water. The company's manager tells the consultant to leave it out of the report to avoid bad publicity. What should the consultant do?
options: Leave it out of the report, because the duty to the client who pays for the work comes first
Publish the details online so the public can protect itself straight away
Escalate it in writing and press for a fix, using proper legal routes if needed
Fix the control system quietly without telling anyone at the company
question.explanation: Public safety under Canon 1 ranks above duty to a client under Canon 3, so silence is wrong. Publishing is tempting, but it arms attackers and is not responsible behaviour. The proper route protects the public and stays honest and legal.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A client tells a security consultant to sign a report stating that a control was tested on a date when no test took place. The client hints that the contract may end if the consultant refuses. What should the consultant do FIRST?
options: Sign the report this once and carry out the missing test a little later, so the record becomes true
Decline to sign and explain in writing why that date cannot be stated
Sign the report but keep a private note of what really happened in case of a later dispute
Report the client to the police before speaking with anyone at the company
practiceQuestions.explanation: A false statement breaks Canon 2, which ranks above service to a client under Canon 3, so the consultant refuses and records why. Testing later is tempting, but the report would still state something untrue.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security manager is asked to lead a review of the control systems in a chemical plant. The manager is skilled in office networks but has never worked with plant equipment. Which action BEST follows the ISC2 Code?
options: Accept the work and learn about plant equipment during the review, charging only half of the normal fee
Accept the work, since the manager's certification covers every kind of technology
Refuse all involvement and give the client no further advice about the plant
Explain the skill gap and bring in a qualified specialist
practiceQuestions.explanation: Canon 3 requires competent service, so the manager is open about the gap and arranges real expertise. Charging less is tempting, but a lower fee does not make unskilled work safe for a chemical plant.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A new member is preparing a short talk for colleagues on how to decide between competing duties under the ISC2 Code. Which order, from highest to lowest, should the talk present?
options: Society, honesty and law, principals, profession
Principals, society, honesty and law, profession
Honesty and law, society, profession, principals
Society, principals, profession, honesty and law
practiceQuestions.explanation: The canons run from society, to honest and legal behaviour, to principals, to the profession. Putting principals first is tempting because they pay you, but duty to the public and to the law ranks higher.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company asks its security manager to help choose a new firewall supplier. One of the suppliers on the shortlist is partly owned by the manager's brother. What should the manager do?
options: Stay on the panel and score that supplier a little lower, so that nobody can claim favouritism
Stay on the panel without saying anything, because the manager knows the decision will be fair
Declare the interest and step out of the decision
Ask the brother to sell his share in the company before the final decision is announced
practiceQuestions.explanation: This is a conflict of interest, which must be declared and removed from the decision. Scoring the supplier lower is tempting, but that is still biased, and it treats the supplier unfairly.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A woman with no link to a company reads that a certified consultant gave that company careless service. She wants to file an ISC2 complaint under Canon 3. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: She may file it, because any member of the public may complain under every one of the four canons
She may not file it, because only principals may complain under Canon 3
She may file it only if she also holds a current ISC2 certification
She may not file it, because complaints can only be made by the police or by a court
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only principals, meaning employers or clients, may complain under Canon 3. The public may complain under Canons 1 and 2. The first option is tempting, but it ignores this limit.

practiceQuestions.prompt: While checking a monitoring tool for signs of malware, an analyst notices that a captured message from a colleague appears to discuss a medical condition. The message has nothing to do with the malware. What should the analyst do?
options: Leave it unread and carry on only with the authorized task
Read it to confirm that it is harmless, then tell the colleague that it was captured by the system
Pass it to the colleague's manager, who may need to arrange support for a staff member's health
Save a copy in a restricted folder in case it turns out to be useful evidence at a later date
practiceQuestions.explanation: Access should go no further than the authorized purpose, and honourable conduct respects private information. Telling the manager may sound caring, but it spreads private data with no authority to do so.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An executive instructs a security engineer to install hidden tracking software on staff phones. The company has no policy allowing this, and local law requires staff to be told. What is the engineer's BEST response?
options: Install it as told, because the executive is responsible for the instruction and its legal results
Install it on a small group of phones first and see whether anyone complains about it
Refuse and immediately warn every member of staff by email about the executive's plan
Hold off and raise the legal issue with management and legal advisers
practiceQuestions.explanation: Canon 2 requires legal behaviour, and the engineer should raise the concern through proper channels before doing anything. Warning all staff is tempting, but it skips the process and may be based on incomplete facts.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A colleague preparing for the CISSP exam sends you a link to a site that claims to list questions copied from the live exam. What should you do?
options: Use the site for a short time, because every candidate looks for extra study material of this kind
Forward the link to your study group so that nobody in the group is at a disadvantage on the day
Do not use it, and report it through the proper ISC2 channel
Post the link on a public forum and warn others that the site exists and is being used by candidates
practiceQuestions.explanation: Using or spreading exam content harms the value of the credential, which goes against Canon 4. Warning people on a forum is tempting, but it advertises the site, while a report to ISC2 reaches those who can act.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has just published a code of ethics, but early surveys show that staff think it applies only to junior employees. What would MOST improve the code's effectiveness?
options: Leaders follow it visibly and it is enforced fairly at all levels
The code is rewritten by outside lawyers, using more precise and more detailed language throughout
The code is printed on posters and placed in every office and meeting room in the building
Junior employees are asked to sign the code a second time at their next yearly review
practiceQuestions.explanation: Staff follow what leaders do, so visible commitment and fair enforcement address the real problem. Better wording is tempting, but the survey shows a trust problem and not a drafting problem.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a contract competition, a bidder offers the security manager on the evaluation panel a free holiday, with nothing said about the bid. What is the BEST course of action?
options: Accept the holiday, because the bidder has not asked for anything in return
Decline it and report the offer as the company's code requires
Accept the holiday only after the contract has been awarded and the competition has formally closed
Decline it without telling anyone, so that the bidder is not embarrassed in front of the panel
practiceQuestions.explanation: A valuable gift during a competition creates a conflict of interest, even when nothing is asked. Declining in silence is tempting, but the panel needs to know, so the offer must be reported.

topics.name: Core security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, nonrepudiation
topics.simpleExplanation: Almost all of security aims at five goals. Confidentiality keeps secrets from the wrong people. Integrity keeps information correct and unchanged. Availability makes sure things work when people need them. Authenticity means something is genuine, and really comes from who it claims. Nonrepudiation means a person cannot later deny they did something. Think of a signed letter in a sealed envelope, delivered on time. Every control you study later supports at least one of these goals. When you read an exam question, ask which goal is at risk.

studyNotes.heading: The five goals, and confidentiality
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to meet the five goals that almost all security work serves, and then look closely at the first one.

The five goals are confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity and nonrepudiation. The first three are known together as the CIA triad. Here CIA stands for confidentiality, integrity and availability. It has nothing to do with spies. A triad is simply a group of three.

A useful picture is a signed letter in a sealed envelope, delivered on time. Keep that in mind, because each part of it matches one goal.

Confidentiality means that only allowed people can see the information. The sealed envelope gives you confidentiality. In your own life, your bank balance should be seen by you and the bank, and not by your neighbour.

At work, think of a payroll file. Only the payroll team should be able to open it. If a salesperson can browse everyone's salary, confidentiality has failed, even though nothing was changed and the system kept running.

There are several ways to protect confidentiality. Encryption scrambles data so that only someone with the right key can read it. Access control decides who may open what. Data classification labels information by how sensitive it is, so that people know how to handle it. Training matters too, because people can leak information by accident.

The threats are just as varied. Laptops are stolen. Network traffic is secretly read, which is called eavesdropping. Someone reads your screen from behind you, which is called shoulder surfing. An employee emails a file to the wrong person.

Confidentiality is related to privacy, but they are not the same. Confidentiality is about keeping any kind of information from the wrong people. Privacy is about a person's right to control their own personal information.

When you read an exam question, ask yourself which goal is at risk. If the worry is the wrong person seeing something, the goal is confidentiality.

So here is what to take away. Confidentiality means only the right people can see the information, and a failure can happen without anything being changed or broken.

studyNotes.heading: Integrity
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at integrity. This goal is about whether you can trust that information is correct.

Integrity means that information stays accurate and complete, and that it is only changed by allowed people in allowed ways. Back in our letter, the fact that nobody has altered the words on the page is integrity.

Here is an everyday example. A teacher writes a mark of 40 in the register. A student sneaks in and changes it to 90. Nobody saw anything secret, and the register is still available. But the record is now false, so integrity has failed.

It helps to think about integrity in three parts. First, stop unauthorized people from making changes. Second, stop authorized people from making changes they should not make. Third, keep information consistent, so that the records inside a system agree with each other and with the real world.

The second part surprises people. Imagine a warehouse clerk who is allowed to update stock figures. If that clerk records stock that does not exist, in order to hide a theft, the person was authorized, but the change was not. Integrity has failed.

The tools for integrity are different from those for confidentiality. A hash is a short fingerprint of data, worked out by a mathematical formula. If even one letter changes, the fingerprint changes. So you can compare fingerprints to find out whether a file has been altered. A hash does not hide the data, and it does not say who made it.

Other tools include digital signatures, which we will come to soon, and change control, which means changes are requested, approved and recorded. Input checks reject values that make no sense, such as a date of birth in the future. Separation of duties, which splits a task between people, makes false entries harder.

A workplace case: a bank's payment file is altered so that money goes to the wrong account. Encrypting the file would not by itself tell you it was altered.

Remember this as your takeaway. Integrity means information can be trusted as correct, and that covers honest mistakes and insiders as well as attackers.

studyNotes.heading: Availability
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at availability, the third part of the triad. This goal is about whether things work when people need them.

Availability means that systems and data are ready and reachable for authorized people at the time they are needed. In our letter picture, this is the part about being delivered on time. A perfect letter that arrives a week late is of no use.

Think of a cash machine that is always broken. Your money is safe and the balance is correct, but you cannot get to it. In daily life that feels like a security failure, and it is one.

In a workplace, imagine a hospital that loses access to patient records during a power cut. Nobody has stolen anything. Nothing has been altered. But doctors cannot see which drugs a patient is allergic to. Lack of availability can put lives at risk.

Availability is threatened by many things that are not attacks at all. Hardware fails. Floods happen. Someone cuts a cable while digging a road. An update goes wrong. There are attacks as well, such as denial of service, where a system is flooded with so much traffic that real users cannot get in. Ransomware, which locks your files and demands payment, is also an attack on availability.

The tools are about having a spare and a way back. Backups are copies that let you restore data. Redundancy means having more than one of something important, such as two power supplies or two internet links. Good capacity planning makes sure a system can handle its busiest day. Maintenance and patching, which means applying software fixes, keep systems healthy.

Availability is often measured as a percentage of time. Here is a worked example. There are about 8,766 hours in a year. A service promising 99.9 percent availability may be down for one tenth of one percent of the year. That comes to just under nine hours a year. A promise of 99.999 percent allows only about five minutes a year. Each extra nine costs much more money.

Here is the takeaway. Availability means being there when needed, and it is threatened by accidents and failures as often as by attackers.

studyNotes.heading: Authenticity and nonrepudiation
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at the last two goals, authenticity and nonrepudiation. People often mix these up, so we will go carefully.

Authenticity means that something is genuine and really comes from where it claims. A letter that truly came from your bank is authentic. A forged one is not.

Do not confuse authenticity with authentication. Authentication is the act of proving who you are, such as entering a password. Authenticity is the quality of being genuine. One is something you do. The other is something a thing has.

Nonrepudiation means a person cannot successfully deny having done something. To repudiate means to deny. Your handwritten signature on a contract gives this in the paper world. You cannot easily claim later that you never agreed.

In the digital world, the main tool is the digital signature. It is made with a private key, which is a secret value held by only one person. Others check the signature using the matching public key, which anybody may have. If the check passes, three things are shown. The message came from the holder of the private key, which is authenticity. The message has not changed, which is integrity. And the signer cannot easily deny it, which is nonrepudiation.

The list of what a signature does not give is just as important. It does not give confidentiality. Anyone may still read a signed message. If you want secrecy as well, you must also encrypt it.

Now here is a point the exam likes. Nonrepudiation needs something tied to one person only. A key shared by two people cannot give it, because either of them could have used the key. A shared user account fails for the same reason.

Consider a workplace case. Four finance clerks all log in using one account called finance. A false payment is approved. The log shows the account, but it cannot show which person acted. Individual accounts and good logs would solve that.

So take this away. Authenticity is about being genuine, nonrepudiation is about not being able to deny, and both depend on tying actions to one identity.

studyNotes.heading: The opposite view, and reading a scenario
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to turn the goals around and look at them from the attacker's side. Then we will practise working out which goal a situation is really about.

DAD is a short way of remembering what attackers try to cause. It stands for disclosure, alteration and destruction. Each one is the opposite of a part of the CIA triad.

- Disclosure attacks confidentiality.
- Alteration attacks integrity.
- Destruction, or denial, attacks availability.

Here is an everyday way to hold this. Imagine your diary. If your sister reads it, that is disclosure. If she writes false entries in it, that is alteration. If she burns it, that is destruction.

The exam rarely asks you to recite these words. It describes something that happened, and expects you to identify the goal. So let us work through some examples together.

A stranger copies a customer list and sells it. Nothing was changed, and the list is still there. The goal harmed is confidentiality.

An employee edits a supplier's bank details in the payment system to divert money. The data is now wrong. The goal harmed is integrity.

A ransomware attack locks the hospital's records so staff cannot open them. The first goal harmed is availability. If the attackers also copied the records first, confidentiality has been harmed as well.

A fake website copies your bank's login page. The site is not what it claims to be. The goal harmed is authenticity.

A manager approves a purchase and later says it was never approved, and no record can show otherwise. The goal that was missing is nonrepudiation.

There is a useful habit here. Look at the actual effect in the scenario, not the method used. A question may mention a firewall, encryption or harmful software to distract you. Ask only one thing. What went wrong for the business? Was something seen, changed, lost, faked or denied?

Here is what to remember. Seen is confidentiality, changed is integrity, lost is availability, faked is authenticity, and denied is nonrepudiation.

studyNotes.heading: Balancing the goals
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at why you cannot simply maximize all the goals at once, and how an adviser chooses the right balance.

Think about your front door. You could fit ten locks. Burglars would struggle, but so would you, especially when you are carrying shopping or need to get out during a fire. More protection in one direction can cost you something in another.

The same is true at work. Strong encryption protects confidentiality, but if the key is lost, the data is unreachable, and availability has suffered. Long approval chains protect integrity, but they slow the business down. Keeping many copies of data helps availability, but each copy is one more thing that could leak.

The right balance depends on what the organization does. A newspaper website publishes articles for everyone, so confidentiality of those articles hardly matters. Availability and integrity matter a great deal. A false story under the paper's name would be a disaster. A defence ministry's battle plan values confidentiality above nearly everything. A hospital's records need all three, and in an emergency, reaching a patient's record quickly can save a life.

Here is a worked example of the thinking. A hospital is considering a login step that takes one minute each time. Step one, ask what the hospital exists to do, which is to care for patients. Step two, identify the goals in tension, which are confidentiality and availability. Step three, ask how much harm a delay could cause, and how much harm unauthorized viewing could cause. Step four, find a control that serves both, such as a fast badge login for clinicians, together with an audited emergency access route that is reviewed afterwards.

That is the adviser's mindset. You do not defend one goal blindly. You find out what the organization needs, you explain the trade-offs, and you let the people who own the risk make the decision. When people's lives are at stake, safety decides.

So here is your takeaway. The goals compete with one another, the business mission sets the balance, and human safety outranks everything else.

topics.memoryHook: A signed letter in a sealed envelope, delivered on time: sealed is confidential, untouched is integrity, on time is availability, the real sender is authentic, and the signature means no denying it.

question.prompt: A company has a dispute with a manager who says she never approved a large payment. The company wants to stop this kind of dispute in future. Which control would BEST meet this need?
options: Encrypting all payment files while they are stored on the server
Having each approver sign payments with a personal private key
Keeping an approval log for one shared finance team account
Calculating a hash of every payment file each night
question.explanation: The need is nonrepudiation, and a personal private key ties the approval to one person. A log is tempting, but a shared account cannot show who acted. Encryption gives secrecy, and a hash only shows whether a file changed.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A delivery company discovers that a dispatcher has been changing delivery records to hide parcels that went missing on his route. He was allowed to edit those records as part of his job. Which security goal has been harmed MOST directly?
options: Confidentiality, because the dispatcher looked at customer records in the course of his daily work
Availability, because the correct delivery information can no longer be used by the business
Integrity, because the records are now false
Nonrepudiation, because the dispatcher might deny having made the changes if he were asked about them
practiceQuestions.explanation: Integrity also covers improper changes made by authorized people, so false entries harm integrity. Nonrepudiation is tempting, but nothing in the scenario says that he denied it or that his actions cannot be traced.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A law firm needs to send a contract to a client. The client must be able to confirm who sent it and that it has not been altered, but the contract is not secret. Which control BEST meets the need?
options: A digital signature made with the sender's private key
Encrypting the contract with a password that is sent to the client in a separate message on the same day
Sending the contract over an encrypted connection to a shared folder used by both of the firms
Publishing a hash of the contract in the text of the same email that carries the document
practiceQuestions.explanation: A digital signature shows who signed and that nothing changed, and secrecy is not needed. A hash in the same email is tempting, but anyone who alters the document could also alter the hash.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A shared account is used by six engineers to administer a production database. An important table is deleted and each engineer says someone else did it. What is the BEST long-term fix?
options: Change the shared account's password each week and give the new password only to senior engineers
Restore the table from backup and ask the engineers to be much more careful in future
Keep database logs for a longer period so that the investigation team has more data to search
Give each engineer an individual account with logging
practiceQuestions.explanation: Accountability and nonrepudiation need actions to be tied to one person. Longer logs are tempting, but logs of a shared account still cannot show which engineer acted.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Staff at a company receive an email that looks as if it came from the payroll team, but it was sent by an outsider using a look-alike address. Which security property of the email is MOST clearly missing?
options: Availability
Authenticity
Confidentiality
Nonrepudiation
practiceQuestions.explanation: The message is not genuine, so authenticity is missing. Nonrepudiation is tempting, but that concerns a real sender being unable to deny sending something, and here the claimed sender did not send it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A hospital's ransomware investigation shows that files were encrypted so that staff could not open them. There is no evidence that any data left the network. Which goal was harmed MOST directly?
options: Authenticity
Confidentiality
Availability
Nonrepudiation
practiceQuestions.explanation: Staff could not reach the data, so availability was harmed. Confidentiality is tempting because the word encrypted is usually linked with it, but here encryption was the attacker's method for denying access.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A software company wants customers to be able to confirm that a downloaded update really came from the company and was not modified. A developer suggests publishing the file's hash on the download page. What is the MAIN weakness of relying only on that?
options: A hash can only be calculated for small files and would not work with larger update packages
A hash makes the file unreadable to customers who have not been given a decryption key by the company
A hash slows the download so much that availability is put at serious risk for most customers
An attacker who controls the page can replace both the file and the hash
practiceQuestions.explanation: A plain hash shows change only if the hash itself can be trusted, and it does not identify the source. A digital signature solves both problems. The other options describe things a hash does not do.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A news organization is setting priorities for its public website, which carries only articles meant for everyone to read. Which pair of goals should it value MOST for those articles?
options: Confidentiality and nonrepudiation
Integrity and availability
Confidentiality and availability
Confidentiality and integrity
practiceQuestions.explanation: Public articles do not need secrecy, but they must be correct and reachable. Pairs that include confidentiality are tempting because it is the most familiar goal, but it adds little for content meant for everyone.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two companies exchange orders, and each message carries a check value created with a secret key that both companies share. One company later denies sending a particular order. Why can the check value NOT settle this dispute?
options: Either company could have created the value
The check value does not show whether the order was altered in transit between the two companies
A shared secret key can only be used to protect stored data and cannot be used on messages
The check value provides confidentiality only and offers no assurance of any other security goal
practiceQuestions.explanation: Both parties hold the same key, so the value cannot prove which one created it. Nonrepudiation needs a key held by one party. The second option is wrong, since a keyed check does show alteration.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A web shop's security team proposes making customers pass four separate login checks for every purchase. Sales staff warn that customers will leave. What should the security adviser do FIRST?
options: Support the four checks, because stronger login always reduces the total risk faced by the company
Drop the proposal, because customer sales are always more important than any security measure
Apply the checks for one month and then see whether the sales figures have fallen
Work out the actual risk and business impact so that the owners can decide
practiceQuestions.explanation: Controls must fit business needs, and the adviser gives decision makers the facts. A one-month trial is tempting, but it risks real losses and still does not show which level of control the risk justifies.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company stores all of its customer data encrypted, and only one administrator knows where the single copy of the decryption key is kept. What is the GREATEST concern with this arrangement?
options: Confidentiality, because encrypted data can usually be read without the key by anyone who has physical access
Integrity, because encryption changes the contents of files in a way that makes them permanently unreliable
Availability, because losing the key would make the data unreadable
Authenticity, because encryption of stored data removes any record of where the data first came from
practiceQuestions.explanation: A single key known to one person is a single point of failure, and the data could be lost for good. Confidentiality is tempting because encryption is involved, but the encryption is actually protecting it here.

topics.name: Security governance principles
topics.simpleExplanation: Governance means how leaders direct and oversee an organization. Security governance makes sure security helps the business reach its goals. Security must also fit changes such as buying or selling a company. Everyone needs a clear role, and the top leaders stay responsible. Many organizations follow a published control framework, which is a ready-made guide to good security. Two ideas are tested often. Due diligence is researching, planning and checking. Due care is doing the right thing in practice. A wise leader does both.

studyNotes.heading: Aligning security to the business
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at the most important idea in governance, which is that security exists to serve the business.

Governance means how leaders direct and oversee an organization. It answers questions like who decides, who pays, and who checks. Security governance applies those questions to security.

The outline uses four words that sound alike, so let us separate them. The mission is why the organization exists. A hospital's mission is to care for patients. The strategy is the broad plan for achieving that mission over several years. Goals are the outcomes it wants along the way, such as opening a new children's ward. Objectives are specific and measurable targets, such as treating patients within four hours of arrival.

A security program must fit all four. Here is an everyday picture. A bodyguard for a pop star does not lock the star in a safe room. The star's job is to appear in public. The bodyguard works out how to make that possible and safe. A good security leader thinks in the same way.

Now a workplace example. A retail chain plans to start selling online within a year. A poor security manager says that online selling is too risky, and blocks it. A good one asks what the plan needs. Then the manager proposes secure payment handling, fraud checks and customer data protection, and estimates what they will cost. Security has become part of how the strategy succeeds.

This is also why a small school and a large bank need very different security. Their missions, their risks and their budgets are different.

On the exam, this idea appears in a simple way. When an answer protects things perfectly but stops the business from doing its work, that answer is usually wrong. When an answer begins by understanding what the business needs, it is often right.

So here is what to take away. Learn what the business is trying to achieve first. Security is successful when it helps the organization reach its mission at a level of risk that its leaders accept.

studyNotes.heading: Top-down direction and levels of planning
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at how security direction flows through an organization, and the three levels at which security is planned.

Governance works from the top down. Senior leaders set direction, approve policy, and provide money and people. Think of a family planning a long journey. The parents decide where the family is going and how much can be spent. The children can suggest things, but they cannot book the flights.

In an organization, a security program that starts at the bottom usually fails. An enthusiastic technician can install tools, but cannot make the finance director follow the rules. Without senior support, a security program lacks authority and budget. When a scenario describes a program that nobody follows, the first thing to look for is management support.

The security function also needs enough independence. If the security leader reports only to the head of technology, there can be a conflict. That head of technology may prefer to deliver projects quickly, and may not want to hear about their risks. Many organizations give the security leader a route to the chief executive, or to the board.

Plans are written at three levels, and you should know the usual time scales.

- Strategic plan: long-term, often about five years.
- Tactical plan: mid-term, often about one year.
- Operational plan: short-term and detailed, such as this month's tasks.

Here is a worked example. A bank's strategic plan says that it will move to a model where every access request is checked, over five years. Its tactical plan says that this year it will roll out stronger login for all staff, and it sets a budget for that. Its operational plan says that next week the help desk will enrol the two hundred people in the Kingston branch.

Each level feeds the one below it, and results at the lower levels report back up.

Here is your takeaway. Direction comes from the top. Senior support is the first thing a security program needs, and plans run from long-term strategic, through mid-term tactical, to short-term operational.

studyNotes.heading: Organizational processes
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at organizational processes. These are the big business events that can change risk very quickly. The outline names three: acquisitions, divestitures and governance committees.

An acquisition is when one company buys another. Think about buying a used car. You would look under the bonnet first. You would want to know about hidden rust before it becomes your problem. Buying a company works the same way, and when you buy it, you also buy its weaknesses.

So in an acquisition, security should be involved before the deal closes. You review the other company's policies, past incidents, legal duties, contracts and technology. You assess whether it may already have been breached. You keep the networks apart until that work is done. Then you connect them carefully, in stages. You also have to deal with two sets of rules, and decide which ones will apply.

A divestiture is when part of a company is sold or closed. The risk runs in the opposite direction. Think of a couple separating and sharing out the house keys. You must be sure who still has a key.

In a divestiture, you decide which data goes and which stays. You remove access for people who are leaving with the sold business. You clean or transfer equipment properly, so that no data is left behind. You also close any network links that are no longer needed. Contracts may require certain services to continue for a time, so the separation must be planned with care.

A governance committee is a group of leaders from different departments who review security decisions and priorities. It usually includes people from the business, technology, legal, finance and human resources. Here is why that matters. A committee gives security support across the company. It also stops one department from making decisions that affect everyone else. It may approve policies, review major risks and settle budget priorities.

So remember this. Business change is a security event. Assess before you connect, clean up when you separate, and use a cross-department committee to keep decisions visible and supported.

studyNotes.heading: Roles and responsibilities
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at who does what in security. The exam often tests whether you know the difference between being accountable and doing the work.

Here is the most important fact. Senior management is ultimately responsible for security. Leaders can hand out tasks, but they cannot hand away the final responsibility. Think of the captain of a ship. The captain may sleep while an officer steers, but if the ship runs aground, the captain answers for it.

The Chief Information Security Officer, or CISO, leads the security program and advises other leaders. The CISO builds the program, reports on risk and asks for resources. Senior management still decides how much risk the organization will accept.

Security professionals design, build and run the controls. A control is anything that reduces risk.

A data owner is a manager who is accountable for a set of data. The owner decides how it is classified and who should be allowed to use it. In a hospital, the head of the records department may own patient records. Note that the owner is a business manager, and usually not a technical person.

A data custodian carries out the daily care of the data. This is often someone in the technology team who runs backups and applies the access rules. The owner decides. The custodian does.

Users must follow policy and report problems. Auditors check independently that controls are working, and they report to management. Independence is what makes an audit worth having. Auditors should not audit their own work, and they do not fix what they find.

Here is a workplace example. A database of customer orders has no clear rule on who may view it. The database administrator asks who should have access. The answer should come from the data owner, who is probably the head of sales or customer service. The administrator then applies that decision.

So here is what to take away. Senior management holds final responsibility. Owners decide, custodians carry out, auditors check independently, and the CISO advises and leads the program.

studyNotes.heading: Control frameworks
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at control frameworks. You do not have to memorize their contents, but you should know what each one is for.

A control framework is an organized set of security practices. Think of a recipe book compared with cooking from memory. It saves you from inventing everything and forgetting something important. Here are the ones to recognize.

- ISO 27001, from the International Organization for Standardization: a standard for an information security management system. An organization can be certified against it.
- ISO 27002: guidance on the controls themselves.
- Special Publication 800-53, from NIST, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology: a large catalogue of controls.
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework: six functions, which are Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
- COBIT, or Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology: governance and management of company technology.
- SABSA, or Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture: security design built from business needs.
- PCI DSS, or Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: protection of payment card data.
- FedRAMP, or Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program: security of cloud services used by the US government.

The key to telling them apart is the clue in the question. If an organization wants a certificate to show to its customers, think of ISO 27001. If it wants a very detailed list of controls, think of NIST 800-53. If its board wants technology to deliver business value under good management, think of COBIT. If an architect wants to build security from business requirements downward, think of SABSA. If it takes credit cards, PCI DSS applies. If it wants to sell cloud services to US federal agencies, it needs FedRAMP.

Here is a workplace example. A software firm wants to win contracts with large European customers who keep asking for proof of good security. The best fit is usually ISO 27001 certification.

Here is your takeaway. Frameworks save you from starting from nothing. Match each one to its purpose, and tailor it to the organization rather than copying it blindly.

studyNotes.heading: Due care and due diligence
studyNotes.body:
In this last part, we are going to separate two phrases that are tested often and confused often, due diligence and due care.

Imagine a landlord. Finding out what the fire code demands, planning how to meet it, and checking the alarms each month is due diligence. Actually installing the alarms and repairing the broken stair is due care.

Due diligence is the research, the planning and the checking. It is about knowing what should be done, and making sure it is being done. Due care is taking the reasonable action. It is what a sensible person in the same position would actually do.

A reasonable standard is often called the prudent person rule. Prudent means careful and sensible. The question is what a prudent person would have done in that situation. A leader is not expected to be perfect, but is expected to be reasonable.

Now here is a worked example from a workplace. A company is thinking of using a new payroll provider.

Step one. Before signing, the company reviews the provider's audit reports and its breach history. That is due diligence.

Step two. Based on what it finds, the company requires encryption, which scrambles data so outsiders cannot read it, and a breach notification clause in the contract, and it limits who can reach the data. That is due care.

Step three. Each year, the company checks that the provider still meets those terms. That checking is due diligence again.

Step four. When the provider reports a weakness, the company makes sure it gets fixed. That is due care again.

You can see that the two work together in a cycle. Investigating without acting achieves nothing. Acting without investigating is guesswork.

If leaders fail at either one, they can be found negligent. Negligence means being legally at fault for not taking enough care. Showing that you did both is often the best defence after something goes wrong. Good records are how you show it.

This is the takeaway. Due diligence is finding out and checking. Due care is doing the reasonable thing. A wise leader does both, and keeps the evidence.

keyTerms.meaning: How leaders direct, control and oversee an organization.
One company buying another.
Selling or closing part of a company.
Chief Information Security Officer: the leader of the security program.
An organized, published set of security practices.
Researching, planning and checking what should be done.
Taking the reasonable action to protect people and assets.
Being legally at fault for failing to take reasonable care.

keyPoints: Security must support the goals of the business.
Senior management holds final responsibility and cannot hand it away.
Check a company's security before connecting to it in an acquisition.
Due diligence is planning and checking, and due care is doing.
topics.memoryHook: Diligence is the Detective who studies and checks. Care is the Carpenter who fixes the stair.

question.prompt: A retail company is about to buy a smaller online shop. The technology team wants to connect the two networks next week so that staff can share systems. What should the security manager recommend FIRST?
options: Connect the networks now, then scan the smaller shop's systems afterwards
Ask the shop's staff to change all their passwords on the day of connection
Install a firewall between the networks and allow all traffic for the first month
Assess the smaller shop's security and risks before any connection is made
question.explanation: In an acquisition you can inherit the other company's weaknesses, so assessment comes first. This is due diligence. Scanning afterwards is tempting, but by then any existing compromise could already have spread across the networks.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A newly formed e-commerce firm hires its first security manager. The founders want to launch in three months. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Understand the firm's objectives and what the launch requires
Buy and install a full set of intrusion detection tools so that the launch is protected from its first day
Write a complete set of detailed procedures for all staff, covering every possible type of security incident
Advise the founders to delay the launch until all security work has been completed to a high standard
practiceQuestions.explanation: Security must align to the business, so its plans begin with understanding what the business needs. Advising delay is tempting, but no assessment has yet shown that delay is needed.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A marketing manager asks the database administrator which staff should be allowed to see the customer contact list. Who should make this decision?
options: The database administrator who looks after the system and understands its technical permissions
The internal auditor, who is independent of the department and of the people asking for access
The data owner accountable for the customer list
The help desk team, which handles the access requests sent in by staff across the company
practiceQuestions.explanation: The data owner decides classification and who may use the data. The administrator is tempting because that person has technical control, but a custodian only carries out the owner's decisions.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A multinational company is selling its logistics division to another firm. What is the MOST important security concern as the sale completes?
options: Recruiting new security staff to replace the people who are moving to the buyer's organization
Removing departing staff's access and properly handling data and equipment
Buying a new set of security tools for the parts of the business that remain after the sale
Rewriting the company's security policies so that they refer to the new company structure
practiceQuestions.explanation: In a divestiture, access and data must be separated cleanly so nothing is left exposed. Rewriting policy is tempting and may follow later, but it does not address the immediate risk.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A software company wants to prove its security to prospective customers by showing an independent certificate for its information security management system. Which option BEST fits this aim?
options: COBIT
NIST Special Publication 800-53
SABSA
practiceQuestions.explanation: ISO 27001 is a standard for a management system that organizations can be certified against. NIST 800-53 is tempting since it is well respected, but it is a catalogue of controls and does not provide that certificate.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's chief information security officer finds that each department sets its own security priorities, so that decisions regularly conflict. Which step would BEST address this at a governance level?
options: Require each department to appoint one member of staff to look after its own firewalls and servers
Move all security work to an outside provider so that departments no longer need to make any decisions
Set up a cross-department committee to review priorities and decisions
Send each department head a monthly list of all of the security incidents across the organization
practiceQuestions.explanation: A governance committee brings leaders together to agree priorities and gives security support across the business. Outsourcing is tempting, but accountability and the need for decisions stay with the organization.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company selects a backup provider. It reads the provider's audit reports and inspects past breach records before signing. Which concept does this activity BEST represent?
options: Due diligence
Due care
Risk transfer
Separation of duties
practiceQuestions.explanation: Researching and checking before acting is due diligence. Due care is tempting because the company is behaving responsibly, but due care is the action taken as a result, such as adding contract terms.

practiceQuestions.prompt: After a serious data breach, a regulator asks a bank to show that its leaders acted reasonably. Which evidence would be MOST useful?
options: A statement from the chief executive saying that security has always been a very high priority
A list of all of the security products that the bank has purchased during the last ten years
Press articles showing that many other banks have suffered similar breaches during the same period
Records of risk reviews and actions taken
practiceQuestions.explanation: Documented reviews show due diligence, and documented actions show due care. A list of products is tempting, but owning tools does not show they were chosen, used or checked sensibly.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An internal auditor finds a serious weakness in the access controls for a payments system and is asked by the technology team to fix it directly. What should the auditor do?
options: Fix it, because the auditor already understands the weakness better than anyone else in the company
Report it to management and leave the correction to the responsible team
Fix it, but leave the weakness out of the final report so that the technology team is not blamed
Ignore the request and wait for the next yearly audit to find out whether the problem still exists
practiceQuestions.explanation: Auditors must stay independent, so they report and do not implement fixes. Fixing it is tempting and may seem helpful, but the auditor would then be judging their own work later.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security leader has prepared a program for the year but cannot get departments to follow it. Staff say the program has no authority. What is MOST likely missing?
options: A larger number of technical controls on the company's networks and its staff computers
More security staff based in each of the company's departments and branch offices
Visible support and approval from senior management
A more detailed set of operational tasks for the security team to work through each week
practiceQuestions.explanation: Governance works from the top down, and without senior support a program has little authority. More detailed tasks are tempting, but they do not give the program the backing it needs.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A bank is planning its security work. One document sets out a security direction for the next five years, and another sets this year's projects and budget. Which pair of terms BEST describes these two documents, in that order?
options: Strategic and tactical
Operational and tactical
Tactical and strategic
Strategic and operational
practiceQuestions.explanation: Long-term direction is strategic, and mid-term work of about a year is tactical. Strategic and operational is tempting, but operational plans are short-term and detailed, such as this month's tasks.

topics.name: Compliance, laws and regulations
topics.simpleExplanation: Compliance means obeying the rules that apply to you. Some rules are laws. Others come from regulators, industry bodies or contracts you signed. Security staff must know which rules apply. Privacy laws protect personal information. Intellectual property law protects ideas and creative work. Other laws control which technologies may leave a country, and where data may travel. Cybercrime and data breaches bring their own duties, including telling people when data is exposed. A security professional is not a lawyer, so always involve legal advisers when the law is unclear.

studyNotes.heading: Cybercrime and data breaches
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at cybercrime and data breaches, and at the legal duties that follow from them.

Cybercrime means crime carried out using computers or aimed at computers. It includes hacking into systems, fraud, stealing data, and spreading harmful software. A data breach is when information is seen, copied or stolen by someone who should not have it. Not every breach is a crime, because a clerk who emails a file to the wrong person has caused a breach by accident.

Think about a burglary in your street. If the burglar lives nearby, the local police can deal with it. Now imagine the burglar lives on another continent, and has never set foot in your country. That is the normal situation in cybercrime. It makes jurisdiction hard. Jurisdiction means which country's law and courts apply. Laws differ from one place to another, and something illegal in one country may not be illegal in the next. Some countries have agreed to cooperate. One well-known example is the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime.

A breach also brings duties. Many laws require you to tell a regulator, which is a government body that oversees an area, and sometimes the affected people as well. The deadlines are short and they differ. You will meet one important deadline shortly, when we reach European privacy law.

Here is a workplace example. A retailer finds that customer records have been copied by an outsider. A good response follows the incident plan that was agreed in advance. The team contains the damage and preserves the evidence. Legal advisers are brought in early to work out which laws apply in each country where customers live. Then the company notifies the authorities and the customers as the law requires.

A security professional is not a lawyer. When the law is unclear, involve legal advisers. And never attack back. Trying to break into the attacker's computer is usually illegal in its own right.

So here is what to take away. Cybercrime crosses borders, breaches bring legal notification duties, and the correct first move is to follow your plan and involve legal advisers.

studyNotes.heading: Intellectual property and licensing
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at intellectual property and licensing. Intellectual property means things created by the mind, and the law protects them in four main ways.

- Copyright: protects creative works, including software code. It often lasts for the author's life plus 70 years.
- Trademark: protects names and logos. It can be renewed without limit.
- Patent: protects inventions, usually for 20 years from filing. The details become public.
- Trade secret: protects valuable secret business information. It lasts as long as it stays secret.

Here are everyday pictures for each. A novel is protected by copyright. The name and logo of a soft drink are protected by trademark. A new kind of engine is protected by a patent. And a secret recipe for fried chicken is a trade secret.

The choice between a patent and a trade secret is one the exam likes. A patent gives strong protection, but only for a limited time, and you must publish how the invention works. A trade secret can last forever, but it gives you little protection if someone discovers the secret honestly, for example by working it out independently. So companies protect trade secrets using access limits and non-disclosure agreements, which are promises to keep information secret.

Copyright protects the way an idea is expressed, and not the idea itself. Two programmers may write different code to do the same job, and neither has copied the other.

A licence is permission to use software under certain terms. You usually buy the right to use it, and you do not own it. Common forms are a signed contract, a shrink-wrap licence that you accept by opening the box, a click-through licence that you accept by clicking a button, and cloud service terms. Open source software is also licensed, and its terms can carry real duties.

Here is a workplace example. A company buys 300 licences, but an audit finds 500 installations. That is a violation, and it can bring penalties. Keeping an accurate software inventory prevents this.

The point to take away is this. Know the four types and how long each one lasts, and track your licences carefully.

studyNotes.heading: Import and export controls
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at import and export controls. These are laws that limit which goods and technologies can cross a national border.

Think about customs at an airport. You may carry a suitcase of clothes, but certain items are stopped, even if you bought them legally. Technology faces rules of the same kind, particularly technology that could be useful to a military or to a hostile government.

The United States has two sets of rules that you should recognize.

- International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR: cover military items and defence services.
- Export Administration Regulations, or EAR: cover commercial and dual-use items, including some encryption.

Dual-use means useful for both civilian and military purposes. Encryption means scrambling data so that only someone with the key can read it. A strong encryption product can protect a shopkeeper's records, and it can also protect a military communication. Many countries also take part in the Wassenaar Arrangement. This is an agreement between states to control the export of weapons and dual-use goods.

Imports are controlled as well. Some countries restrict bringing encryption products in, or require a licence to use them, or require access to keys. So a product that is legal at home may not be allowed where you plan to use it.

Here is a worked workplace example. A company in Canada sends an engineer to a new branch office abroad, with a laptop that uses strong encryption and a set of design files. Step one, find out whether the encryption can legally be taken into that country. Step two, find out whether the design files are controlled, because sending technical data can count as an export, even by email. Step three, check who will receive them, since some people and countries are restricted. Step four, get legal or compliance approval, and keep a record.

Notice one trap. Export does not only mean shipping a box. Giving access to controlled technical data over a network can count as well.

This is what to take away. Before technology or technical data crosses a border, find out what the rules allow in both directions, and ask legal or compliance staff before you move it.

studyNotes.heading: Transborder data flow
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at transborder data flow. This means data moving between countries, particularly personal data.

Imagine you hand your medical file to a friend, and the friend passes it to someone in a country where nobody is required to keep it private. You would want some say in that. Data protection laws give people that kind of protection.

Some countries go further and require certain data to stay inside their borders. This is called data localization, or data sovereignty when it is about the country's legal control over the data. A common example is government data, or health records.

The cloud makes this harder. The cloud means computing services run for you by another company over the internet. A cloud provider may copy your data automatically to several regions, for safety. That sounds sensible, but those copies may be crossing borders that your legal duties forbid. So when you buy a cloud service, you need to know where the data will be stored, where it will be backed up, and where the provider's support staff are based.

The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, or GDPR, allows personal data to leave the European area in a few main ways.

- The destination country has an adequacy decision, meaning the European Commission has judged its protection adequate.
- The parties use standard contractual clauses, which are approved contract terms.
- A group of companies uses binding corporate rules, which are approved internal rules for moving data within that group.

These arrangements can change. An earlier framework for transfers to the United States, known as Privacy Shield, was struck down by the European court in 2020. So you cannot assume last year's answer is still valid.

Here is a worked workplace example. A company in France wants to send its staff records to a head office outside Europe. First, map the data and find out where it will go. Next, take legal advice on the lawful basis for the transfer. Then, put the proper safeguards in place. Only after that should the data move.

Here is your takeaway. Know where your data is going, make sure there is a lawful basis for the transfer, and settle it before any data moves.

studyNotes.heading: Privacy requirements
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at privacy. Privacy is a person's right to have a say in how information about them is collected and used.

Personally identifiable information, or PII, is any data that can identify a person, such as a name together with a date of birth. The biggest privacy law you will study is the GDPR. It protects people in the European Union, even when the company handling their data is elsewhere. So a shop in Jamaica that sells to customers in Germany may have to obey it.

Learn these roles. A data subject is the person the data is about. A controller decides why and how data is used. A processor handles data on the controller's behalf. Here is an everyday picture. You are the data subject. Your dentist is the controller. The company that stores the dentist's records is the processor. The controller stays responsible for choosing a good processor.

The GDPR has seven principles. Lawfulness, fairness and transparency. Purpose limitation, which means using data only for the reason given. Data minimization, which means collecting no more than you need. Accuracy. Storage limitation, which means not keeping data longer than needed. Integrity and confidentiality. And accountability, which means being able to show that you comply.

People also have rights, such as seeing their data, correcting it and asking for it to be erased.

The numbers to remember are these. A breach must be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless it is unlikely to harm people. The highest fines reach 20 million euros or 4 percent of worldwide yearly turnover, whichever is higher.

Other laws to recognize are these.

- California Consumer Privacy Act, or CCPA.
- Personal Information Protection Law, or PIPL, in China.
- Protection of Personal Information Act, or POPIA, in South Africa.
- Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, for US health data.
- Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, or GLBA, for US financial customer data.

The takeaway is this. Know the three GDPR roles, the seven principles and the 72-hour rule, and match each law to its place.

studyNotes.heading: Four sources of requirements
studyNotes.body:
In this last part, we are going to bring it together by looking at where requirements come from. The outline names four sources, and the exam expects you to tell them apart.

- Contractual: promises in an agreement. Break them and the other party may sue.
- Legal: laws made by government. Breaking them can bring fines or prison.
- Industry standards: rules set by an industry body.
- Regulatory: rules from a government agency that oversees an area, such as banking.

Think about running a small food stall. The law says you must not sell unsafe food. A health inspector, working for a government agency, has detailed rules about how you store it. A trade association may set its own quality mark. And your contract with a supermarket says you will deliver every Monday. Those are four different kinds of duty, and all four are real.

The example the exam loves is PCI DSS. That stands for Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard. It applies to anyone handling payment cards. It is not a law. It is an industry standard, and card companies enforce it through contracts. If you break it, you can face fines or lose the right to accept cards. Saying that it is not a law does not make it optional.

Another law worth knowing is the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, or SOX. It requires accurate financial reporting by US public companies, and so it drives controls over the systems that hold financial data.

Compliance means meeting the rules that apply to you. A good compliance program lists which requirements apply and who is responsible for each one. It maps controls to those requirements, checks them regularly and reviews the list after any change.

Here is a workplace example. A medical software firm opens a European office and begins taking card payments. In a single move, it picks up privacy law, health data law, an industry standard and new customer contracts. The list must be updated before the launch.

So remember this. Requirements come from contracts, laws, industry standards and regulators. You must know which apply, and involve legal advisers wherever the answer is unclear.

keyTerms.meaning: Meeting the rules that apply to the organization.
Personally Identifiable Information: data that can identify a person.
General Data Protection Regulation: the European Union's main privacy law.
The party that decides why and how personal data is used.
The party that handles personal data for the controller.
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: an industry rule set for card data, enforced by contract.
Valuable business information protected for as long as it stays secret.
Moving data across national borders.
Which country's law and courts apply.
