In this part we will look at two points in a person's working life where access can go wrong: when they arrive, and when they change roles.

Onboarding means bringing a new person in. They receive accounts with least privilege, which means only the access needed for the job. They get security training, and a copy of the policies. They should know who to call about a problem and how to report something suspicious.

Think about a new pupil at a school. On the first day they get a timetable, a locker key and a tour. They do not get the key to the head teacher's office. And somebody explains what to do if the fire alarm rings.

Good onboarding is a repeatable process. A request comes from the hiring manager, it is approved, and the access is set according to the person's role. Keeping a record of what was approved also makes later reviews much easier.

A transfer means moving to a new role within the same organization. Here you must remove old access and add only what the new role needs. If you only ever add access, you get privilege creep, which is the slow build-up of too much access.

Let us work through a workplace example. A woman starts in accounts, with access to the payments system. Two years later, she moves to purchasing. If nobody removes her payment access, she may now be able to both raise a purchase order and pay for it. That defeats separation of duties, even though no one meant it to.

The fix is to build access removal into the transfer process itself. Human resources tells the access team about each move. The old role's access ends, and the new role's access begins. Then a regular access review, in which managers confirm who should have what, catches anything that slipped through.

The exam mindset here is to fix the process and not only the single case. Removing one person's extra access is correct, but it does not stop the next one.

Here is your takeaway. Start people with least privilege, and on every transfer remove the old access, so that privilege creep cannot build up.

studyNotes.heading: Termination
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at termination, which means the end of someone's employment. It can be voluntary, when a person resigns, or forced, when the organization dismisses them.

A forced termination is one of the riskier moments in personnel security. The person may be angry, and may still have the ability to do damage.

Think of ending a shared tenancy after a serious argument. You would want the locks changed at about the same moment as the conversation, not a week before, and not a week afterwards.

For a forced termination, disable all access at the same moment the person is told, or just before. If you disable it long before, you tip them off. If you do it long after, they have time to cause harm.

Hold the meeting with a manager and a witness, usually from human resources, the department that deals with staff matters. Collect badges, keys, phones and laptops. Escort the person from the building. Hold an exit interview where possible, and remind them of the agreements they signed, such as a non-disclosure agreement, which is a promise to keep information secret. Afterwards, check accounts and keep records as required.

Please notice that all of this should be done with respect. A person losing a job is going through a hard moment. Protect people's safety and dignity. Do not humiliate anyone in front of colleagues.

Here is a workplace example of the sequence. A network engineer is being dismissed at two in the afternoon. At that moment, the access team disables the engineer's accounts, which was agreed in advance. Shared passwords the engineer knew are changed. The manager and a human resources officer hold the meeting. Equipment is returned and signed for. Security walks the engineer to the door with personal belongings. Later that day, someone reviews what the engineer did in the final days.

For a voluntary resignation, the risk is usually lower, but it still needs review. Access still ends promptly on the last day.

Here is what to remember. Coordinate access removal with the moment of notice, keep a witness present, recover company property, and treat people with respect.

studyNotes.heading: Vendors, compliance and privacy
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to look at outsiders who work with us, how staff are kept compliant, and the privacy that employees are owed.

Vendors, consultants and contractors are people or companies from outside who do work for you. A vendor sells goods or services. A consultant gives expert advice. A contractor carries out work under a contract. They can have real access to your systems, so treat them with the same care as staff.

Think of a plumber who has a key to your house. You would want a written agreement, and you would want the key back when the job is done.

Use written agreements that cover non-disclosure, security duties, access limits and the right to audit, which means your right to check that they are keeping their promises. Review their access regularly, and end it when the work ends. Linking each account to the contract's end date is a simple and effective control.

Always remember one thing. Your organization stays responsible for its data, even when someone else handles it.

Policy compliance means that staff really do follow the rules. Train them, ask them to acknowledge the policy, monitor behaviour and apply fair, consistent consequences. Managers must follow the rules as well. If the director is excused, staff notice.

Employees also have privacy rights. Tell staff in advance if email, internet use or systems are monitored, for example through a policy and a login banner. A login banner is a notice shown when someone signs in. Collect only the personal data that the job needs, and keep it protected.

Here is a workplace example. A company begins to monitor web traffic, and tells nobody. A year later, it tries to discipline someone based on that monitoring. The employee argues that they had a reasonable expectation of privacy. If the company had published a clear policy and shown a banner, its position would have been much stronger. Laws differ between countries, so legal advisers must be involved.

So here is your takeaway. Treat outsiders with the same discipline as staff, enforce policy fairly, and tell people before you monitor them.

keyTerms.meaning: Checking a person's background before hiring.
Non-Disclosure Agreement: a promise to keep information secret.
Giving only the access needed for the job.
Splitting a sensitive task so one person cannot complete it alone.
People secretly working together to get around a control.
Moving staff through roles to find fraud and build backup skills.
Required time off, so someone else can see the person's work.
Slow build-up of too much access as a person changes roles.

keyPoints: Match screening to the risk of the job, and follow the law.
On a transfer, remove old access before or as you add new access.
For a forced termination, disable access when the person is told.
Tell staff in advance if they are monitored.
topics.memoryHook: Hire with a check, work with a limit, move with a clean-up, leave with a lockout.

question.prompt: An employee who worked in accounts has moved to the marketing team. An access review six months later shows she can still approve payments and also has every marketing permission. What is the BEST long-term fix?
options: Change the transfer process to remove old access at every role change
Remove her payment access and remind her not to use it again
Run a yearly report that lists all staff who changed departments during the year
Move her to a role where the payment access would be useful
question.explanation: This is privilege creep caused by a weak process, so the process must be fixed. Removing her access is tempting and should also happen, but it fixes only one person and not the cause.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company applies an identical light background check to every new hire, including staff who will manage the company's main bank accounts. What should the security adviser recommend?
options: Keep the current process, because treating every candidate the same is the only fair way to hire
Stop checking candidates entirely, so that the company avoids any possible privacy complaints in future
Ask new managers to write their own statement confirming that they have no history of financial wrongdoing
Match the depth of screening to each role's risk, within the law
practiceQuestions.explanation: Screening should fit the risk of the job. Treating everyone identically is tempting because it sounds fair, but fairness means treating similar jobs alike, and high-trust roles justify deeper checks.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A hiring manager wants to run a criminal record check on a preferred candidate. Local law requires the candidate's agreement before this check can be done. What should the manager do FIRST?
options: Run the check quietly through a friend who works for a screening firm, so that the candidate is not offended
Skip the check, on the grounds that the candidate has already interviewed well and has good references
Obtain the candidate's permission and follow the legal process
Run the check, then ask the candidate to sign a form for it once the job offer has been accepted
practiceQuestions.explanation: Screening must follow local law, which here requires permission first. Getting a signature afterwards is tempting since it seems to satisfy the rule, but consent must come before the check.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A product designer is resigning to join a competitor. At the exit interview, which reminder is MOST important from a security standpoint?
options: That the non-disclosure agreement continues to apply
That the company offers a very generous bonus scheme to employees who return within two years
That all staff are expected to complete a satisfaction survey before they leave the building for the last time
That the competitor may not offer as many days of paid holiday as the current employer does
practiceQuestions.explanation: An NDA often continues after someone leaves, and the exit interview is the moment to remind them. The other options may matter to human resources, but they do not protect company information.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A manager plans to dismiss an employee and intends to hold the meeting alone in a private room so as to spare the person embarrassment. What should the security adviser recommend?
options: Carry on as planned, and write up a short note of the discussion at some point later on in the same week
Include a witness, usually from human resources
Send the dismissal by email instead, so that there is no need for any meeting to take place
Ask the employee's closest friend at work to sit in on the meeting and offer personal support
practiceQuestions.explanation: A witness protects both the company and the employee, and it can still be handled with respect. A note afterwards is tempting, but it is only one person's account of what was said.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An audit finds that one accounts clerk can both create new suppliers and approve payments to them. What is the BEST control to add?
options: A yearly reminder to the clerk about the penalties that apply to financial fraud at the company
A security camera positioned above the clerk's desk, so that all of the clerk's activity can be observed
Separating the two tasks between different people
Longer and more complex passwords for all staff who have access to the accounts system
practiceQuestions.explanation: Splitting the task stops one person from committing fraud alone. A camera is tempting because it sounds strong, but it cannot show what the clerk is doing inside the system or prevent the conflict.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A bank suspects that long-hidden fraud may be going on, and it wants someone else to handle each employee's work for two weeks in a row each year, in order to reveal any irregularities. Which control BEST fits?
options: Least privilege
Separation of duties
Non-disclosure agreements
Mandatory vacation
practiceQuestions.explanation: Required time off lets someone else see the work, which helps detect fraud. Separation of duties is tempting, but it splits tasks to prevent fraud, and does not require anyone to take a break.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two warehouse employees, one who records deliveries and one who approves them, secretly agree to approve goods that never arrived. Which term BEST describes what they have done?
options: Privilege creep
Collusion
Job rotation
Repudiation
practiceQuestions.explanation: Collusion is people secretly working together to defeat a control such as separation of duties. Privilege creep is tempting, but that is a slow build-up of access, and the scenario has none.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A review finds that the accounts of several contractors stayed active for months after their contracts ended. What is the BEST long-term fix?
options: Link each contractor account to its contract end date
Disable these particular contractor accounts straight away and send a note to the managers who hired them
Ask all contractors to promise in writing that they will not log in after their final day of work
Have the security team search the system each year for any accounts that were not used over the past year
practiceQuestions.explanation: Automatic expiry fixes the cause, which is that access outlives the contract. Disabling those accounts is tempting and should happen, but it does nothing about the next contractor.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has decided to monitor the websites that its staff visit from work computers. What should be done FIRST, before monitoring begins?
options: Set up the monitoring quietly and see what it reveals before deciding what staff need to know about it
Ask each department manager to choose which members of their team should be watched most closely
Inform staff in advance through policy and a login banner
Buy the most comprehensive monitoring product available, so that nothing is ever missed by the company
practiceQuestions.explanation: Staff should be told about monitoring in advance, and legal advice applied, so that expectations of privacy are clear. Monitoring quietly is tempting for catching wrongdoing, but it creates legal and trust problems.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's outsourced payroll provider suffers a breach that exposes staff data. The chief executive says that the breach is entirely the provider's problem. What is the BEST response from the security manager?
options: Agree, because the contract moved all responsibility for the staff data over to the payroll provider
Agree, but offer to help the provider as a gesture of goodwill between the two companies
Disagree, and arrange to take over the provider's systems and carry out the investigation directly
Disagree, because the company remains accountable for its data
practiceQuestions.explanation: Work can be outsourced, but accountability cannot. Agreeing is tempting because the provider failed, but the company chose that provider and still owes a duty to its staff.

topics.name: Risk management
topics.simpleExplanation: Risk is the chance that something bad will happen and the harm it would cause. Risk management means finding those risks, measuring them and deciding what to do. You can measure risk in words or in money. Then management chooses to reduce it, transfer it, avoid it or accept it. Controls are the safeguards used to reduce risk. They must be checked and monitored over time. Security staff advise, but senior management makes the final decision about how much risk to accept.

studyNotes.heading: Basic words, threats and vulnerabilities
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to learn the basic words of risk management, because every later idea depends on them.

An asset is anything of value. A threat is something that could cause harm, such as a thief, a flood or a careless employee. A vulnerability is a weakness, such as a broken lock. Risk is the chance that a threat will use a weakness, together with the harm that results. Exposure means being open to possible loss. A safeguard, or control, is something that reduces risk.

Here is an everyday picture that joins these together. Your bicycle is the asset. A thief is the threat. Leaving the bicycle unlocked is the vulnerability. The risk is the chance that it will be stolen and what that would cost you. A good lock is the control.

Notice that a threat without a vulnerability causes little harm, and so does a vulnerability with no threat. A flood is no danger to a house on a high hill. Risk needs both.

Now let us look at a workplace. A web server holding customer data is the asset. A criminal group is the threat. An unpatched flaw in its software, meaning a fault that has not yet been fixed, is the vulnerability. The risk is that the data will be stolen.

Threat and vulnerability identification is the first practical stage of the work. You find threats by looking at incident history, industry reports and intelligence from other organizations, and by talking to the people who run the systems. You find vulnerabilities using scanning tools, audits, penetration tests, which are authorized simulated attacks, and reviews of processes.

Always include non-technical threats. Fires, floods, resignations and honest mistakes cause a great deal of real harm.

The risk manager's job is not to remove all risk. That is impossible, and it would be far too expensive. The job is to help the organization understand its risk, and to bring it down to a level that leaders accept.

So here is what to take away. A threat acts on a vulnerability to harm an asset, risk is the likelihood and the harm together, and the aim is to manage risk and not to eliminate it.

studyNotes.heading: Risk analysis and scope
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at how risk is analyzed and how the boundaries of the work are set.

Scope means deciding what the assessment covers. Before you begin, you need to agree which systems, sites and business processes are included. A risk assessment of everything, all at once, usually goes nowhere. Think about tidying a house. You can do one room at a time, and be clear about which room you are doing, or you can feel overwhelmed and do nothing.

There are two main approaches to analysis.

Qualitative analysis uses words or simple rankings, such as high, medium and low. It is often shown as a risk matrix, which is a grid with likelihood on one side and impact on the other. A risk that is both likely and harmful lands in the most serious corner. Qualitative work is quick and easy to understand. Its weakness is that it depends on opinion.

One way to improve those opinions is the Delphi method. It gathers anonymous expert opinions in rounds. Each expert sees a summary of what the group said and can then change their view. Because it is anonymous, the most senior person in the room cannot dominate.

Quantitative analysis uses money and numbers. It gives results that a finance director can compare directly with a budget. Its weakness is that it needs good data, and that data can be hard to find. How would you put an exact figure on the likelihood of a new type of attack?

Most organizations combine the two. A common pattern is a qualitative assessment for all risks, followed by a detailed quantitative look at the few most serious ones.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital ranks fifty risks as high, medium or low in a workshop. Six are high. For those six, it gathers figures on cost and frequency, so that it can compare possible controls.

Remember also that risk assessment is a repeated activity. Things change, and so must the assessment.

Here is your takeaway. Agree the scope first. Qualitative is words and judgment, quantitative is money and numbers, and the two work well together.

studyNotes.heading: The risk maths, with a worked example
studyNotes.body:
Now we come to the arithmetic. It is simple once you know the steps, so let us take one step at a time.

Asset Value, or AV, is what the asset is worth. Exposure Factor, or EF, is the percentage of the asset lost in one event. Single Loss Expectancy, or SLE, is the money lost in one event. Annualized Rate of Occurrence, or ARO, is how many times per year the event is expected. Annualized Loss Expectancy, or ALE, is the expected loss per year.

There are two formulas to know. Say them aloud.

Single loss expectancy equals asset value times exposure factor.

Annualized loss expectancy equals single loss expectancy times annualized rate of occurrence.

Think of a mobile phone. It is worth 400 dollars, and a dropped phone loses a quarter of its value in repairs. So one drop costs 100 dollars. If you drop it twice a year, your yearly bill is 200 dollars. That is the entire idea.

Now a workplace example. A warehouse is worth 500,000 dollars. A flood would destroy 40 percent of it. A flood is expected once in 10 years.

Step one, the single loss expectancy. 500,000 dollars times 0.40 is 200,000 dollars. That is the cost of one flood.

Step two, the rate. Once in 10 years means 1 divided by 10, which is 0.1 per year.

Step three, the annualized loss expectancy. 200,000 dollars times 0.1 is 20,000 dollars per year.

Be careful with the rate. An event that happens four times a year has a rate of 4. An event that happens once in 50 years has a rate of 1 divided by 50, which is 0.02. A rate can be more than one, or much less than one.

One more caution. The yearly figure is an average. The warehouse will not lose 20,000 dollars every year. It will lose nothing for years, and then 200,000 dollars in a single flood. The yearly figure is simply a fair way to compare risks and budgets.

Here is what to take away. Asset value times exposure factor gives one hit, and one hit times how often gives the yearly bill.

studyNotes.heading: Risk response and whether a safeguard is worth it
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at the choices management has, and how to decide whether a safeguard is worth buying.

There are four responses to know.

- Mitigate: reduce the risk with controls.
- Transfer or share: pass the cost to another party, such as through cybersecurity insurance.
- Avoid: stop the risky activity.
- Accept: knowingly live with it, with management's written approval.

Here is an everyday picture. You are going on a long drive. Wearing a seat belt is mitigation. Buying car insurance is transfer. Deciding not to make the trip is avoidance. Accepting that some small risk remains, and setting off anyway, is acceptance.

Ignoring a risk is never acceptable. Rejecting a risk, which means pretending it is not there, is different from accepting it. Acceptance is a conscious and recorded decision.

With transfer, remember that accountability stays with you. If your insurer pays for a breach, your customers still blame you.

Inherent risk exists before controls. Residual risk remains after them. Senior management decides what residual risk to accept.

Now let us see whether a safeguard is worth buying, by carrying on with our warehouse. The annualized loss expectancy today is 20,000 dollars. A flood barrier costs 8,000 dollars a year, and it lowers the annualized loss expectancy to 5,000 dollars.

The value of a safeguard equals the annualized loss before, minus the annualized loss after, minus the yearly cost of the safeguard.

So 20,000 minus 5,000 is 15,000 dollars. That is the saving. Then 15,000 minus 8,000 is 7,000 dollars. A positive result means it is worth buying.

Now change one number. Suppose the barrier costs 18,000 dollars a year. Then 15,000 minus 18,000 is minus 3,000 dollars. The safeguard costs more than it saves. On the numbers alone, you would not buy it.

The yearly cost should include everything, such as purchase spread over its useful life, maintenance and staff time. And if a safeguard protects human life, cost is not the only thing to weigh.

Here is your takeaway. Choose among mitigate, transfer, avoid and accept, and subtract the safeguard's cost from what it saves.

studyNotes.heading: Types of control and control assessments
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the kinds of control there are, and how we test whether they really work.

Controls are grouped by how they work. Administrative controls are policies and procedures. Technical controls, also called logical controls, use technology, such as firewalls, which filter network traffic. Physical controls are things you can touch, such as fences and locks.

Controls are also grouped by purpose.

- Preventive: stops an event. A lock.
- Detective: discovers an event. A camera recording.
- Corrective: fixes things after an event. Removing a virus.
- Deterrent: discourages. A warning sign.
- Recovery: restores operations. Backups.
- Compensating: an alternative when the main control cannot be used.
- Directive: tells people what to do. A policy.

A single thing can be described in both ways. A security guard is a physical control. A guard can also be preventive, detective and deterrent all at the same time.

Think of keeping your home safe. The front door lock is preventive. The doorbell camera is detective. The sign saying that the property is protected is a deterrent. Repairing a broken window is corrective. And staying with a relative while the home is repaired is a recovery measure.

Here is a workplace example of a compensating control. An old machine in a factory cannot support encryption, which is the scrambling of data to keep it secret, and it cannot be replaced yet. The company places it on an isolated network, and restricts who can reach it. That isolation stands in for the missing control.

Control assessments test whether security and privacy controls really work. A control that exists on paper may not be operating. Think about a smoke alarm with no battery. It looks fine until you need it.

Assessments can be done by reviewing documents, by interviewing people and by testing the control. Testing could mean a practice restore of a backup, or an attempt to log in with a disabled account. Privacy controls are assessed in a similar way, asking whether personal data is really handled as promised.

The point to take away is this. Classify controls by how they work and by their purpose, and always test that they really operate.

studyNotes.heading: Monitoring, reporting, maturity and frameworks
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at how risk management carries on over time, and at the frameworks that guide it.

Continuous monitoring and measurement watch risk and controls over time. Think about checking your weight or your blood pressure regularly, and not just once. A control that worked last year may have failed quietly this year.

Reporting shares the results. Internal reporting goes to leaders, in business language. External reporting goes to regulators, customers or auditors, as required.

Continuous improvement means getting better over time. A risk maturity model shows how well an organization manages risk. One common order runs from least to most mature.

- Ad hoc: nothing is planned, and it depends on individual effort.
- Preliminary: early, inconsistent attempts.
- Defined: standard processes exist and are documented.
- Integrated: risk management is part of business decisions.
- Optimized: it is continually improved.

The most important framework to know is the NIST Risk Management Framework. NIST is the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. It has seven steps, in this exact order.

- Prepare.
- Categorize.
- Select.
- Implement.
- Assess.
- Authorize.
- Monitor.

Here is a workplace walk-through. A government agency gets ready by setting context and priorities. It categorizes a new system by how much harm a loss would cause. It selects suitable controls and implements them. It assesses whether they work. A senior official authorizes the system to operate, accepting the remaining risk. Then the agency monitors it from then on.

Other frameworks to recognize are ISO 31000 and ISO 27005, which are international standards on risk. ISO stands for the International Organization for Standardization. COBIT is Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology, which is about governing technology. SABSA is Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture. PCI DSS, the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, protects card data. And FAIR, or Factor Analysis of Information Risk, measures risk in money.

Here is your takeaway. Risk work never finishes. Monitor, report and improve, and know the seven NIST steps in order.

keyTerms.meaning: Something that could cause harm.
A weakness that a threat could use.
Single Loss Expectancy: the money lost in one event. AV x EF.
Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year the event is expected.
Annualized Loss Expectancy: expected loss per year. SLE x ARO.
The risk that remains after controls are in place.
The risk that exists before any controls are added.
Passing the cost of a risk to another party, such as an insurer.
An alternative control used when the main one cannot be used.

keyPoints: SLE = AV x EF, and ALE = SLE x ARO.
The four responses are mitigate, transfer, avoid and accept.
Ignoring a risk is never a valid response.
Senior management decides how much residual risk to accept.
topics.memoryHook: AV times EF gives one hit (SLE). One hit times how often gives the yearly bill (ALE).

question.prompt: After new controls were added, a security manager reports that some risk to the customer database still remains and that further controls would cost more than the possible loss. Who should make the final decision to accept this remaining risk?
options: The security manager who carried out the assessment
The database administrators who look after the system every day
Senior management, with the decision formally recorded
The external auditor who reviews the database each year
question.explanation: Senior management is accountable and decides what residual risk to accept. The security manager is the tempting choice, but that role advises and does not own the business decision.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A server room and its equipment are valued at 200,000 dollars. A fire is expected to destroy 60 percent of that value. What is the single loss expectancy?
options: 80,000 dollars
200,000 dollars
120,000 dollars
12,000 dollars
practiceQuestions.explanation: Single loss expectancy is asset value times exposure factor, so 200,000 times 0.60 is 120,000 dollars. 80,000 dollars is tempting, but that is the 40 percent of value that survives the fire.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has calculated a single loss expectancy of 30,000 dollars for a type of fraud that it expects to suffer four times a year. What is the annualized loss expectancy?
options: 120,000 dollars
7,500 dollars
30,000 dollars
34,000 dollars
practiceQuestions.explanation: Annualized loss expectancy is single loss expectancy times the yearly rate, so 30,000 times 4 is 120,000 dollars. 7,500 dollars is tempting, but that comes from dividing by the rate instead of multiplying.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A building is worth 1,000,000 dollars. An earthquake would destroy half of its value, and one is expected every 25 years. What is the annualized loss expectancy?
options: 500,000 dollars
20,000 dollars
40,000 dollars
12,500 dollars
practiceQuestions.explanation: One event costs 1,000,000 times 0.5, which is 500,000 dollars. The rate is 1 divided by 25, which is 0.04. So 500,000 times 0.04 is 20,000 dollars. 500,000 dollars is tempting, but it is the cost of a single event.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A risk has an annualized loss expectancy of 40,000 dollars. A safeguard costing 35,000 dollars a year would lower that figure to 10,000 dollars. Based only on these figures, what should the security manager recommend?
options: Buy it, because it would save 30,000 dollars a year in expected losses
Buy it, because its yearly value is 5,000 dollars
Buy it, because any safeguard that lowers the annual loss will always be worth having
Do not buy it, because it costs 5,000 dollars more than it saves
practiceQuestions.explanation: The saving is 40,000 minus 10,000, which is 30,000 dollars. Subtract the 35,000 dollar cost and the value is minus 5,000 dollars. The first option is tempting, but it leaves out the safeguard's cost.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company buys a cybersecurity insurance policy to cover the cost of a possible data breach. Which risk response does this represent?
options: Transfer
Mitigation
Avoidance
Acceptance
practiceQuestions.explanation: Insurance passes the cost to another party, which is risk transfer. Mitigation is tempting because the company is reducing a worry, but the likelihood of a breach is unchanged, and accountability remains with the company.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A financial firm decides to stop offering an old online service, because the risk of running it is too high and fixing it would cost more than the service earns. Which risk response is this?
options: Transfer
Mitigation
Avoidance
Acceptance
practiceQuestions.explanation: Stopping the risky activity is avoidance. Mitigation is tempting because the risk does go down, but mitigation means keeping the activity and adding controls to it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An old system cannot be upgraded to meet the company's encryption standard. The company places it on an isolated network and limits who can reach it until it can be replaced. What type of control is the isolated network in this case?
options: Deterrent
Detective
Directive
Compensating
practiceQuestions.explanation: It is an alternative used when the main control cannot be applied, so it is compensating. Deterrent is tempting because it limits who can reach the system, but it does more than discourage an attacker.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A shop reviews its camera footage each morning, to find out whether anything happened overnight. Which control purpose BEST describes this review?
options: Preventive
Detective
Corrective
Directive
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reviewing footage finds events after they happen, so it is detective. Preventive is tempting because cameras may put some people off, but that effect would be deterrent, and the review stops nothing.

practiceQuestions.prompt: After adding firewalls, encryption and staff training, a company asks how much risk it still faces in its online store. What is this remaining amount of risk called?
options: Residual risk
Inherent risk
Total exposure factor
Single loss expectancy
practiceQuestions.explanation: The risk left after controls is residual risk. Inherent risk is tempting, but that is the level before any controls are added.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A government team following the NIST Risk Management Framework has just finished implementing the controls that were selected for a new system. What is the NEXT step?
options: Monitor
Authorize
Assess
Select
practiceQuestions.explanation: The order is Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor, so Assess follows Implement. Authorize is tempting, but an official needs the results of the assessment before accepting the risk.

topics.name: Threat modeling
topics.simpleExplanation: Threat modeling means thinking like an attacker before an attack happens. You study a system, ask what could go wrong, and plan defences while changes are still cheap. Imagine walking around your house, noticing every door and window a burglar could use. Several methods help. STRIDE gives a list of threat types. PASTA is a seven-stage process tied to business risk. DREAD gives threats a score, so you can fix the worst first. The best time to begin is early, at the design stage.

studyNotes.heading: What threat modeling does
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at what threat modeling is, and why it should happen early.

A threat is anything that could cause harm. Threat modeling is a structured way to find threats to a system and to decide what to do about them. Put simply, you think like an attacker before an attacker arrives.

Imagine walking around your own house in the evening. You check each door and window. You notice that the back gate does not lock, and that a ladder is lying beside the garage. You have not been burgled. But you have worked out how you might be. Then you do something about it.

Threat modeling can be proactive, which means done during design, before problems exist. It can also be reactive, which means done on a finished system. Proactive is cheaper and better. It is far easier to move a doorway on the drawing than after the walls are built.

Here is a workplace example. A company is designing a mobile banking app. During design, the team notices that a password reset could be requested by anybody who knows a customer's email address. Changing the design at this stage takes an afternoon. Finding the same problem after a million customers are using the app would be far more costly, and it might only be discovered through an attack.

There are different starting points for your thinking.

- Assets: what are we protecting?
- Attackers: who might attack us, and why?
- Software: where is the system itself weak?

An asset-focused approach begins with what is valuable. An attacker-focused approach begins with the people likely to attack you, along with their skills and motives. A software-focused approach begins with the design of the system. All three are useful, and teams often combine them.

Threat modeling also helps a manager. It gives a documented list of risks, so that leaders can decide what to fix first and what to accept.

Here is what to take away. Threat modeling means finding what could go wrong before it does, and the earlier it begins, the cheaper the fixes will be.

studyNotes.heading: The common steps, and trust boundaries
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at how a threat modeling exercise usually runs, and at one concept that makes it much easier, the trust boundary.

Here are the common steps, in order.

- Identify the assets and the goals.
- Draw how the system works, often as a data flow diagram.
- Identify the threats.
- Rate them.
- Decide on responses and record them.

A data flow diagram is a simple picture showing how information moves through a system, from one part to another. Drawing the system breaks it into smaller parts, and this is called decomposition.

When breaking down a system, look at five things. These are trust boundaries, data flow paths, input points, privileged operations and the security approach used. Privileged operations are actions that need special rights, such as changing a password for another user.

A trust boundary is a line where the level of trust changes. Picture a nightclub. Outside the door, anyone may be standing. Past the doorman, people have shown their identification. Past the rope at the VIP area, they have shown something more. Each of those lines is a trust boundary. The checks happen at the lines.

In a computer system, the classic trust boundary lies between the internet and your internal network. Another lies between a web server and the database behind it. Data that crosses from a less trusted zone into a more trusted one must be checked.

Let us work through an example. An online shop has a browser, a web server and a database. Step one, the assets are customer details and payment data. Step two, you draw the three parts, and the arrows between them. Step three, you look at the arrow from the browser to the web server, since this crosses from the internet. What if someone sends a false price, or a harmful command? Step four, you rate how serious that would be. Step five, you record a response, such as checking all input and calculating prices on the server.

The point to take away is this. Draw the system, find where trust changes, and pay the closest attention to data crossing those lines.

studyNotes.heading: STRIDE
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at STRIDE, the best-known way to classify threats.

STRIDE came from Microsoft. Each letter stands for a type of threat, and each one breaks a security goal. It is a checklist that prompts you to think of the kinds of thing that can go wrong.

- Spoofing: pretending to be someone else. Breaks authenticity.
- Tampering: changing data without permission. Breaks integrity.
- Repudiation: denying an action. Breaks nonrepudiation.
- Information disclosure: exposing data. Breaks confidentiality.
- Denial of service: stopping access for real users. Breaks availability.
- Elevation of privilege: gaining more power than allowed. Breaks authorization.

Authorization is the control over what you are allowed to do. Authenticity means being genuine. Integrity means being correct and unchanged. Nonrepudiation means a person cannot deny an action. Confidentiality means only allowed people can see information. Availability means being ready when needed.

Let us bring these to life, using a school. A pupil phones the office and pretends to be a parent. That is spoofing. A pupil changes a grade in the register. That is tampering. A pupil says they were never told about the homework, and no one can prove otherwise. That is repudiation. A pupil reads out the test answers to the class. That is information disclosure. A pupil jams the lock on the classroom door, so that no one can get in. That is denial of service. And a pupil gets hold of the head teacher's keys and starts giving orders. That is elevation of privilege.

Now a workplace example, with an online banking service. An attacker steals a session token, which is the value that shows you are logged in, and acts as a real customer. That is spoofing. A user changes the account number in a request. That is tampering. A user makes a transfer and later denies it, and there are no logs. That is repudiation. An error message reveals account details. That is disclosure. A flood of requests takes the service down. That is denial of service. An ordinary customer reaches an administrator page. That is elevation of privilege.

Here is your takeaway. STRIDE names six kinds of threat, and each one matches a security goal.

studyNotes.heading: PASTA
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at PASTA, which works quite differently from a simple checklist.

PASTA means Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis. It is risk-centric, which means it connects threats to business impact. It does not just ask what could go wrong. It asks what could go wrong that would hurt the business, and how much.

It has seven stages, in this order.

- 1. Definition of objectives.
- 2. Definition of technical scope.
- 3. Application decomposition and analysis.
- 4. Threat analysis.
- 5. Weakness and vulnerability analysis.
- 6. Attack modeling and simulation.
- 7. Risk analysis and management.

Notice the shape of it. It begins with the business. It moves into the technical detail. Then it studies the attacks. And it ends back at the business, with decisions about risk.

Think of planning security for a large public event. First, you decide what success looks like, which is everyone getting home safely. That is your objective. Then you define the site, including its entrances and streets. That is your scope. Next you break it down into areas, such as stage, food stalls and exits. Then you consider who might cause trouble. Next you look for weak points, such as a gate with no steward. Then you walk through how someone could actually get in. Finally, you decide what extra stewards and barriers are worth paying for.

Here is a workplace example. A bank wants to assess a new loans application. In stage one, the bank states that the goal is to protect customer funds and to meet regulatory duties. In stage two, it lists the servers, software and links involved. In stage three, it maps how a loan request moves through the system. In stage four, it looks at the attackers targeting banks at the moment. In stage five, it lists known weaknesses. In stage six, it simulates likely attacks against the application. And in stage seven, it works out the business impact and decides which fixes come first.

The method takes more effort than a checklist, but its results speak the language that leaders use.

Here is what to remember. PASTA has seven stages in fixed order, and it begins and ends with business risk.

studyNotes.heading: DREAD
studyNotes.body:
In this part we are going to look at DREAD, which helps you rank threats by giving them a score.

A list of threats is useful, but a team cannot fix everything at once. DREAD gives a score to each threat, so that you can rank them. Each letter is a question.

- Damage: how bad would it be?
- Reproducibility: how easily can it be repeated?
- Exploitability: how easily can the attack be carried out?
- Affected users: how many people are hit?
- Discoverability: how easily can it be found?

Here is an everyday comparison. Suppose you have two problems with your house. A window on the top floor does not lock. A front door lock can be opened with a butter knife, and everybody on the street knows it. The front door scores higher on nearly every question, so you fix that first.

Let us work through a numeric example. Rate each item from 1 to 10.

Threat one is a flaw in a login page that reveals every customer's data. Damage is 8. Reproducibility is 9. Exploitability is 7. Affected users is 10. Discoverability is 6. Add them together. 8 plus 9 is 17. Plus 7 is 24. Plus 10 is 34. Plus 6 is 40. So the total is 40 out of 50. That is high priority.

Threat two is a rare error on an internal report page, which only staff can reach. Damage is 4. Reproducibility is 2. Exploitability is 3. Affected users is 5. Discoverability is 2. That adds up to 16 out of 50. That can wait.

This gives you a clear order of work, and something to show to management.

DREAD has a known weakness. The scores depend on the opinions of those who give them. Two teams could easily rate the same threat quite differently. You improve this by agreeing what each number means before you start.

Notice the difference between STRIDE and DREAD. STRIDE helps you find and name a threat. DREAD helps you decide how much it matters. They work well together.

Here is your takeaway. DREAD has five questions, its scores rank threats, and those scores are only as consistent as the people giving them.

studyNotes.heading: Other methods, and keeping the model current
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at three other methods you should recognize, and then at how threat modeling should continue over time.

VAST stands for Visual, Agile, Simple Threat. Agile development means building software in small, frequent steps. VAST is designed to fit that way of working at large scale, across many teams. If a scenario mentions many agile teams and a need for threat modeling that keeps pace with them, think of VAST.

Trike focuses on risk and on what each person is allowed to do with each asset. It builds a model of who may create, read, update or delete what, and then looks at what could break those rules. It ties this to a level of risk that stakeholders find acceptable. A stakeholder is anybody with an interest in the outcome.

Attack trees are a diagram with the attacker's goal at the top and the ways to reach it as branches. Think of a family tree turned upside down. At the top is the goal, such as getting into the safe. Beneath it are the branches: pick the lock, steal the key, or trick the manager. Beneath steal the key are smaller branches, such as breaking into the manager's car. Each path from a leaf to the top is one possible attack. You can mark which branches are cheap or easy, and that shows you where the defence matters most.

Here is a workplace example of keeping a model current. A payments company produced a threat model two years ago for its website. Since then, it has added a mobile app and a link to an outside partner. Both of those add new data flows and new trust boundaries. So the old model no longer describes the real system.

Threat modeling is not a one-time job. Repeat it when the system changes. That includes new features, new connections, a new hosting arrangement, or news of a new kind of attack that may apply to you.

As a manager, make it a normal step in the development process, and keep the results where the team can use them.

So here is what to take away. Match the method to the need: VAST for agile scale, Trike for allowed actions, attack trees for paths, and repeat the work whenever the system changes.

keyTerms.meaning: A structured way of finding threats to a system and planning responses.
Done early, before a problem happens.
A line where the level of trust changes.
Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis: a seven-stage, risk-centric method.
Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability: a scoring method.
Visual, Agile, Simple Threat: a method built for agile development at scale.
A diagram showing an attacker's goal and the ways to reach it.

keyPoints: Start threat modeling early, during design.
STRIDE classifies threats, and DREAD scores them.
PASTA has seven stages and ties threats to business risk.
Repeat threat modeling whenever the system changes.
topics.memoryHook: STRIDE names the danger. DREAD measures the danger. PASTA is the seven-course meal that ties it all to the business.

question.prompt: During a design review of an online shop, the team notes that an attacker could change the price of an item in the message sent between the customer's browser and the server. Which STRIDE category BEST describes this threat?
options: Spoofing
Tampering
Repudiation
Elevation of privilege
question.explanation: Changing data without permission is tampering, and it breaks integrity. Spoofing is tempting because attacks often involve fake identity, but here the attacker changes data and does not pretend to be anyone.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is about to begin building a new customer portal. A project manager asks when threat modeling will give the MOST value. What should the security adviser say?
options: After the first release, once real customers have started to show how the system is actually used
During design, before the building work begins
Just before go-live, when all of the features are finished and can be tested in their final state
Only after a security incident has shown that the portal has some weaknesses worth looking at
practiceQuestions.explanation: Starting at design lets the team change things while it is still cheap. Just before go-live is tempting, because the system is complete, but changes at that stage are costly and disruptive.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attacker steals a logged-in customer's session value and uses it to act as that customer on a banking site. Which STRIDE category does this BEST represent?
options: Tampering
Repudiation
Elevation of privilege
Spoofing
practiceQuestions.explanation: Acting as another person is spoofing, which breaks authenticity. Elevation of privilege is tempting, but the attacker has only the customer's rights and has not gained greater power than that user.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A staff member with an ordinary account changes a value in a web address and finds that she can now use the site's administrator functions. Which STRIDE category BEST fits?
options: Spoofing
Denial of service
Elevation of privilege
Information disclosure
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gaining more power than allowed is elevation of privilege. Spoofing is tempting, but she is still using her own account and is not pretending to be another person.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An online store has no record of which user placed a particular order. A customer claims that the order was never placed. Which STRIDE threat does this weakness MOST directly allow?
options: Repudiation
Tampering
Information disclosure
Denial of service
practiceQuestions.explanation: Without a record, the customer can deny the action, which is repudiation. Tampering is tempting because order data is involved, but nothing here says that the data was changed.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A team using PASTA has just finished breaking the application down and mapping how it works. Which stage should come NEXT?
options: Attack modeling and simulation
Risk analysis and management
Definition of technical scope
Threat analysis
practiceQuestions.explanation: Application decomposition is stage three, and threat analysis is stage four. Attack modeling is tempting, but it is stage six, after threats and weaknesses have been studied.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Using DREAD with a score of 1 to 10 for each item, Threat A scores 9, 6, 8, 7 and 5. Threat B scores 5, 5, 4, 6 and 5. Which should be dealt with first, and why?
options: Threat B, because its total of 25 is lower
Threat A, because its total of 35 is higher
Threat A, because its total of 30 is higher
Threat B, because its total of 35 is higher
practiceQuestions.explanation: Threat A adds up to 35 and Threat B adds up to 25, and the higher total goes first. The other options either rank the lower score first, or add up the numbers incorrectly.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A large software company has many development teams, all working in short agile cycles. It wants a threat modeling method designed to scale with this way of working. Which method BEST fits?
options: VAST
PASTA
DREAD
Trike
practiceQuestions.explanation: VAST is built for agile development at large scale. PASTA is tempting, because it is a full method, but it is a heavy staged process and is not designed around agile cycles.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A team wants a threat modeling approach built around what each user is allowed to do with each asset, tied to a level of risk stakeholders accept. Which method BEST fits?
options: STRIDE
An attack tree
Trike
VAST
practiceQuestions.explanation: Trike models allowed actions on assets and acceptable risk. An attack tree is tempting since it is also a modeling tool, but it maps paths to an attacker's goal and does not start with permissions.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A design shows a web server that receives requests from the internet and then sends queries to an internal database. Where should a threat modeling team pay the CLOSEST attention to input checks?
options: Inside the database, on the tables that hold the least important reference information
Between two internal reporting tools that share the same server and the same administrators
On staff workstations, since the people who use them have completed security training
Where internet traffic crosses into the web server
practiceQuestions.explanation: Data crossing a trust boundary from a less trusted zone needs the closest checking. The internal options are tempting to include, but the largest change in trust occurs at the internet boundary.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A threat model was completed two years ago for a payments website. The company has since added a mobile app and a link to a new partner. What is the BEST next step?
options: Keep the existing model, because the core business of taking payments has not changed since it was written
Update the threat model to cover the new changes
Schedule a new threat model for the next time that there is a serious incident on the website
Ask the partner to confirm that its own systems are safe and leave the existing model as it is
practiceQuestions.explanation: New features and connections add data flows and trust boundaries, so the model must be updated. Asking the partner is tempting, but it covers only one part and leaves the model out of date.

topics.name: Supply chain risk management
topics.simpleExplanation: A supply chain is every company and step involved in giving you a product or service. If any link is weak, you can be harmed. A restaurant can serve bad food because a supplier sent bad meat. In security, hardware may be faked or altered, software may carry hidden flaws, and service providers may be careless. Reduce the risk by assessing suppliers, watching them over time, setting minimum security requirements and agreeing service levels. Remember that your organization stays accountable for its data, even when someone else handles it.

studyNotes.heading: What a supply chain is, and why it matters
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at what a supply chain is, and why it has become such a serious security concern.

A supply chain is every company and every step involved in giving you a product or service. Supply chain risk management, or SCRM, means finding and reducing risk from the companies you buy from, and from the companies they buy from.

Think about a restaurant. The chef may be excellent and the kitchen may be spotless. But if a supplier sends bad meat, customers still get sick, and they will blame the restaurant. The restaurant's safety depends on the farm, the transport firm and the warehouse, even though it does not run any of them.

Here is the question to carry with you. Who touched this before it reached me?

At work, think about a laptop. Its parts come from many factories in several countries. Its software comes from different developers, and much of that software includes open source components. Open source means software whose code is publicly shared, and which is often written by volunteers. Then the laptop passes through a warehouse, a delivery firm and perhaps a reseller. Any of these could be a weak link.

There is a reason attackers like this route. Why attack a thousand well-protected companies one by one, when you can attack the one supplier they all trust? An update from a trusted supplier is usually installed without a second thought. So a single compromised update can reach thousands of organizations at once.

This makes the supply chain a problem for managers as well as for technical staff. Decisions made by people buying things can create or reduce risk. Procurement, the department that buys goods and services, should work closely with legal and security staff from the start of any purchase.

The outline for this objective has two halves. One covers the risks of acquiring products and services. The other covers how those risks can be reduced. We will take them in that order.

So here is what to take away. A supply chain includes everyone upstream of you, you inherit their weaknesses, and you should always ask who touched something before it reached you.

studyNotes.heading: Tampering, counterfeits and implants
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the three risks the outline names. They are tampering, counterfeits and implants. We will also look at risks in software and services.

Tampering means someone changes a product before it reaches you. Think of a jar of food with a broken seal. It might be fine, but you have no way of knowing. At work, a shipment of routers may arrive with broken security seals, or with packaging that has been opened and taped up again.

Counterfeits are fake parts sold as real ones. They may fail early or hide bad features. Think about a fake designer handbag that falls apart after a month. At work, a company may buy network equipment at a suspiciously low price from an unknown online seller. The labels look right, but the serial numbers are not on the manufacturer's records. Fake parts are a problem for reliability as well as for security.

Implants are hidden chips or code added to equipment. An implant is deliberately placed to give someone a secret way in, or to send data out. Think of a hidden microphone sewn into a gift. These are very hard to find, and they tend to be used against particularly valuable targets.

The difference is worth stating clearly. A counterfeit pretends to be a different product. Tampering changes a genuine product. An implant is a specific kind of hidden addition.

Software has similar risks. Malicious code can be added during the build or in an update. Open source parts inside a product may contain vulnerabilities, which are weaknesses that attackers can use.

Services carry risks of their own. A cloud provider, meaning a company that runs computing services for you over the internet, may have weak security, poor recovery plans, or staff with too much access. The same is true of a support provider. A provider may also use subcontractors that you do not know about.

Here is a workplace response. When a package arrives, inspect it and check seals. If something looks wrong, set the item aside, contact the maker through a known route, and do not connect it to your network.

The point to take away is this. Tampering alters the real thing, counterfeits imitate it, and implants hide something inside it. Buy from trusted sources, and inspect what arrives.

studyNotes.heading: Third-party assessment and monitoring
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at how you check a supplier, both before you sign and afterwards.

A third party is an outside company that you work with. The rule is simple. Assess it before you sign, and keep checking afterwards.

Think about hiring a babysitter. You ask for references before the first evening. But you also keep paying attention over time, asking the children how it went, and noticing whether anything has changed.

There are several ways to assess a supplier. You can send a questionnaire about its security. That is cheap, but the answers are the supplier's own words. You can review independent audit reports. Or you can carry out on-site audits and tests, where the contract allows it.

One of the most useful reports is a System and Organization Controls report, known as a SOC report. There are three main kinds.

- SOC 1: controls that affect financial reporting.
- SOC 2: controls for security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy. Detailed, and shared in confidence.
- SOC 3: a shorter public version of that report.

These also come in two types. A Type 1 report looks at whether controls are well designed at a single point in time. A Type 2 report looks at whether they actually operated over a period, often a year. So Type 2 is stronger evidence, because it shows that the controls worked over time.

An ISO 27001 certificate from the International Organization for Standardization is another useful sign. Check what its scope covers. A certificate may apply only to one office, and not to the service you are buying.

Monitoring means continuing to check. A supplier that was safe last year may not be safe today. Watch for news of breaches, changes of ownership and missed service levels.

Here is a workplace example. A company signed with a software supplier three years ago, after a careful review. Since then, the supplier has been bought by another company, and most of its staff have left. Nothing in the old review reflects that. It is time to assess again.

Here is your takeaway. Assess before you sign, prefer independent evidence over promises, and keep monitoring afterwards.

studyNotes.heading: Minimum requirements and service levels
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at how you put your expectations in writing. There are two items from the outline here: minimum security requirements and service level requirements.

Minimum security requirements are the lowest level of security a supplier must meet to do business with you. Put them in the contract. A promise made over lunch is worth very little when something goes wrong.

An everyday picture would be a landlord's conditions for a tenant. The tenant must have insurance, must not change the locks without permission, and must report damage right away. Those are the conditions for being allowed to live there.

In a supplier contract, these often include encryption, which scrambles your data so outsiders cannot read it, limits on who can reach it, background checks on staff, a duty to report breaches quickly, and the right to audit. The right to audit means you may check whether the supplier is meeting its promises. Contracts should also flow these requirements down to subcontractors, so that the protection does not stop at the first company in the chain.

A Service Level Requirement, or SLR, describes what the customer needs. A Service Level Agreement, or SLA, is the formal promise from the provider, often with penalties if it is missed. Typical measures are uptime, response time and repair time.

Think about ordering a birthday cake. Saying that you need it by four o'clock on Saturday is your requirement. The bakery's written promise to deliver it by then, with a refund if it is late, is the agreement.

Here is a worked example. A shop needs its payment service up 99.9 percent of the time. That is its SLR. The contract then says the provider will meet 99.9 percent or pay a credit. That is the SLA. Let us see what that really means. A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes. One tenth of one percent of that is about 43 minutes. So the shop is accepting up to about 43 minutes of downtime each month.

Always do the sum. Numbers that look very high may allow more downtime than the business can bear.

Here is what to remember. Put minimum security in the contract, flow it down the chain, and know that an SLR is the need and an SLA is the promise.

studyNotes.heading: Silicon root of trust and physically unclonable functions
studyNotes.body:
In this part we are going to look at two technical protections built right into hardware. They sound difficult, but the ideas are quite simple.

A silicon root of trust is a security function built into a chip. It starts first and checks that the rest of the device's software is genuine and unchanged. Silicon is what computer chips are made of. Root of trust means the starting point that everything else depends on.

Think of a chain of people passing a message. Each person checks the identity of the next. But somebody has to be first, and the whole chain depends on that first person being honest. A silicon root of trust is that first person, and it is built into the chip, so it is much harder to change than ordinary software.

Here is how it works in practice. When a server is powered on, the root of trust checks the first piece of startup code. It verifies a digital signature on that code, which proves who made it and that it has not changed. That code checks the next piece, and so on. If a check fails, the device can stop or raise an alert. So if someone has tampered with the software during shipping, the problem can be detected the first time the device starts.

A physically unclonable function, or PUF, uses tiny, natural differences made in each chip during manufacture. These work like a fingerprint and are extremely hard to copy.

Think about your own fingerprints. Nobody designed them, and even identical twins have different ones. Nobody can simply manufacture a copy of you. In the same way, no two chips come out exactly the same, even from the same factory line. The chip's tiny differences can be measured and used to create a unique identity, or a secret key, without having to store that key in memory.

That last point is important. A key that is never stored in memory is much harder to steal.

A workplace use is identifying genuine devices, which helps to catch counterfeits.

Here is your takeaway. A silicon root of trust checks that startup software is genuine, and a PUF gives each chip a unique identity that is very hard to copy.

studyNotes.heading: Software bills of materials, and the management view
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to look at the software bill of materials, and then pull the whole topic together from a manager's point of view.

A software bill of materials, or SBOM, is a list of all the parts inside a piece of software, like the ingredients on a food label. If you have a nut allergy, you read the label. You do not have to phone the factory.

Modern software is built largely out of parts that other people wrote. So a product you buy may include hundreds of smaller components, and you may have no idea what they are.

Here is a workplace example. A serious flaw is announced in a common file compression component. A company has eighty applications from various suppliers. Without SBOMs, it must write to every supplier and wait for answers. With SBOMs, somebody can search the lists and have a good answer within minutes. Then the most exposed systems can be fixed first.

An SBOM has limits. It tells you what is inside. It does not tell you whether the flaw can actually be used in that product. And it has to be kept up to date with every new release.

Now let us step back. Here is the management view, which the exam cares about most.

You can outsource the work, but you cannot outsource accountability. If a supplier loses your customers' data, your customers will still hold you responsible, and so will the regulators.

So a good manager does several things. Involve procurement, legal and security staff from the start of any purchase. Rank suppliers by how much harm they could do, and give the most attention to the riskiest. Put the requirements in the contract. Check that they are being met. And plan what happens if a supplier fails or is breached, including how you would leave that supplier and get your data back.

If a scenario offers one option that relies on a supplier's assurance and another that verifies it independently, the verified one is usually better.

So here is what to take away. An SBOM tells you what is inside software, and even when work is outsourced, accountability stays with you.
